title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Contagion Engines
content:
In our Detachment Focus series we take a deep dive into an army’s Detachments, covering what’s in them, how they play, and how they’ll fit into the broader meta and your games. In this Detachment Focus we’re looking at the Contagion Engines Detachment for the Death Guard.

The Death Guard received three new 1 DP Detachments at the onset of 11th edition, each of which catered to a different unit type in the army. Of these, the Contagion Engines Detachment focuses on the faction's Bloat-Drones and Blight-Hauler units, giving them a solid boost.

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Reconnaissance

Death Guard armies have leaned heavily on Bloat-Drones and Blight-Haulers since the publication of their tenth edition Codex. They're fast, versatile units with decent durability and some solid damage output for their cost. The Contagion Engine Detachment gives them a much-needed boost by giving them the [ASSAULT] keyword on their ranged attacks.

In addition to this, there is one downside to the Detachment: Namely that it has the ENGINES tag, and can't be taken with another detachment with the ENGINES tag, which means you can't combine this with Mortarion's Hammer, blunting your ability to otherwise take a really sick vehicle Detachment. We're not sure that was necessary, given how Hammer tends to be less of a "vehicle horde" detachment normally and more of a "backdoor method of deep striking Deathshrouds" but it's something to think about.

Detachment Rule: Warped and Rusted Animus

Friendly Bloat-Drone, Helbrute, and Blight-Hauler units have the CONTAGION ENGINE keyword. Friendly CONTAGION ENGINE units have [ASSAULT] on their ranged attacks.

This is pretty good! It’s a nice mobility boost on your bloat-drones and blight-haulers and really helps the former make the most of the changes to the FLY rule, since now they can move through walls by taking a -2” penalty and negate that by simply getting a 2+ on their Advance roll. This is also great because these are units you just want to take - running a list with three Blight-Haulers and three Heavy Blight Launcher Bloat-Drones is more than reasonable, and having extra movement will make your opponent work harder to stay out of melta range.

Despite being among the fastest units in your army, Drones and Haulers only move 10" and getting an extra +3" or +4" is a really solid boost you can use to peak around ruins and close the gap on detection ranges. Every extra inch of movement in Death Guard counts. This is less interesting on Helbrutes, if only because their shooting is just not great.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

Both of these go on vehicles, which is cool.

  • Parasitic Woe-Reaper (15 pts, Upgrade). CONTAGION ENGINE unit only. When this unit has fought, one model in the unit heals D3 wounds. This is a neat little bonus for your Fleshmowers, who are the most likely unit to end up with this upgrade. Healing tends to be better the tougher a unit is, and while T9 10 Wounds, 3+/5++ isn’t crazy, it’s also still solid enough to be annoying. It can also be fun on Blight-Haulers, whose bite attacks benefit from the +1 to hit/wound against MONSTER and VEHICLE targets.
  • Lancet of the Worldsore (15 pts, Upgrade). Goes on a Helbrute or Blight-Hauler. That unit gains MOBILE. This goes a long way to making Helbrutes playable, since being able to burst through a wall Kool-aid man style can help you stay hidden until it’s time to really do some damage. One of the better things about Helbrutes is their small model size - they’re just small enough to still hide. This can also go on a unit of two Blight-Haulers to get more out of the little engines, and combines well with the ASSAULT ability.

Stratagems

  • Fresh Vectors (1 CP). Used in your Shooting phase or the Fight phase, when you pick a Contagion Engine to attack. It can re-roll wound rolls of 1 for the rest of the phase. This is neat, it’s a small but helpful effect for a nice buff when you need it. It's another ability that will do more work if you take units of two Blight-Haulers, since you get double the value out of the Stratagem.
  • Bloodrust Deluge (1 CP). Used in your Shooting phase, when a Contagion Engine shoots. You can pick a visible enemy unit and that unit is Afflicted until your unit has attacked. This one is essentially made with the understanding that you’re taking Rattlejoint Ague in your games, and it’s great for that. Dropping -1 T and -1 Sv on a target from a longe distance can be huge.
  • Soulrot Flux (1 CP). Used in your opponent’s movement phase when they make a Fall back move from an engaged Contagion Engine unit. Roll a D6, and on a 1, they take 1 mortal wound, on a 2-5 they take D3, and on a 6, they take 3 mortal wounds. This is situational but really useful for those times you charge a vehicle and it stays alive on 1-2 wounds.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

This Detachment incentivizes you to play with larger units of Blight-Haulers, pairing them up to get more out of the Lancet of the Worldsore upgrade and the Fresh Vectors Stratagem.

Your biggest problem with this Detachment is that it doesn't pair with anything good; in an ideal world you'd be able to pair it with Virulent Vectorium (already 3 DP) or Hammer of Mortarion (ENGINES tag), to build something that has real cross-unit synergy. So your real options are basically either Shamblerot Vectorium for a Recon strategy that goes wide with Poxwalkers to flood the board or pairing with something like Champions of Contagion to supplement a plague marine-heavy strategy.

The extra movement here on drones and MBHs makes them great, mobile units for scooting around the table, but the sauce here is Bloodrust Deluge - tagging an enemy unit from 36" away before you light it up with a Defiler is a solid value, though you can also get that out of a unit of Plague Marines as well. The thing about this Detachment is that it boosts units most lists were already taking - HBL Bloat Drones were already one of the game's better units, and the Blight-Haulers are likewise just incredibly efficient for their cost. Which is to say that these lists look just like Champions of Contagion or Shamblerot lists, only with stronger small vehicles.

Strengths

  • Great movement buffs for some of the army's best units
  • Decent Stratagems for offensive output and healing

Weaknesses

  • Doesn't pair with Hammer of Mortarion and so no natural pairing options

A Sample List

This list was run in mid July by Jensen Simmons, who finished 5-1 with it at the Hee Yaw event in mid July. It predates the late July balance update, and so will need to be reconfigured to accommodate the increased points cost on the Defiler, which probably ends up costing you one of the two Tallymen in terms of cuts you'll make.

As we mentioned earlier - this is just a regular Death Guard list, but with faster Contagion Engines. And that's more or less how it goes with this Detachment. You have more speed than before on your drones, and this packs a double unit of MBH instead of two single-model units to get more out of the Stratagems, but otherwise not much has changed.

Final Thoughts

If you're running Death Guard and you're not taking Vectorium, this is a solid option. That said, Paragons of Putrescence has been crowding it out recently - you just get more value out of the Terminator upgrades there than you do out of ASSAULT on your contagion engines here. But both detachments share a common factor, which is that they're improving units you just take in every list.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Kinfire Delve
content:
Today, we are taking a look at Kinfire Delve, a cooperative dungeon delving card game that was published by Incredible Dream Studios in 2023 and 2024. It's shares the studio's unique setting–the World of Kinfire–with two other games that are complete separate from Kinfire Delve aside from the world. However, if you're familiar with any of them, then you'll see familiar faces as you explore the various systems. Since this is the first (and so far only) Kinfire game I've played, I'm going to focus solely on it in this review.

I am always on the lookout for cooperative two-player games to play with my lovely wife and other assorted gaming friends. Kinfire Delve was one that I saw mentioned a few times online and was also highly recommended by a friend (thanks, Bryce!), so I decided to give it a shot. The art design was a large factor in my decision, as well. It's a refreshingly bright game with colorful characters and an art style I really vibed with. Seriously, just check out the box and card art throughout this article. The physical cards are also of exceptional quality cardstock and have gold foiling. It gave me premium boardgame material vibes at a surprisingly low price point.

Something else that was readily apparent after breaking into the game was just how easy it is to pick up and play. I'm fairly deep into the weeds of gaming, as you might guess given that I write for a website dedicated to tabletop games, but I've taught the game to people who run the whole spectrum of gaming knowledge. From people with boardgame libraries that would rival what you'd see at a major convention to more casual dabblers to people who are brand new to the boardgame or tabletop world, everyone has been able to quickly pick up the mechanics. More importantly, I've seen every player have some kind of "ah-ha!" moment while playing which is such a positive thing to experience as a player. This game feels like a great fit for the dedicated boardgame crowd, but also for families with differing game skill levels or a group of friends who can vibe with the fantasy theme but might not know the difference between a d8 and a d12.

Kinfire Delve supports anywhere from 1-4 players, provided you have picked up enough of the box sets. This is as good a time as any to go into how Kinfire Delve is packaged. There are three distinct boxes you can pick up for Kinfire Delve and each of them will contain the cards to play as two of the heroes (known as Seekers in the setting), all the cards for one of the big bad guys and their lair (referred to as a Well and the Well Master), and all the relevant tokens and dice you'll need to play. This means if you want to play with only one or two players, you can get by with a single box. If you want to play with more players or mix-and-match the Seekers, you can do so by grabbing two or three boxes. Considering these range around $20-$25 per box, that was an easy pill for me to swallow so I promptly snagged all three of them.

Releases

Vainglory's Grotto, the first Kinfire Delve box set. Credit: Jake Bennington

The first of the three releases for Kinfire Delve, Vainglory's Grotto, was released in 2023. In this box, you'll find Vainglory herself. There is a very strong otherworldly fae court theme to this Well Master which I always enjoy seeing. The first of the Seekers in this box is Khor (they/them), a sort of reborn soul that is housed in a mechanical body. They are accompanied by a cute little moth critter named Flickers that shows up on a bunch of their cards. Mechanically, Khor has methods of reducing incoming damage which is quite helpful given the relatively small shared health pool among the Seekers. The other Seeker is Asha (she/they), an elf assassin who is more effective when going after challenges that already have some progress on them. Asha has tricks including a few more ways to outright discard challenges than the other Seekers -- this comes in handy!

Scorn's Stockade, the second Kinfire Delve box set. Credit: Jake Bennington

The following release was Scorn's Stockade in early 2024. The titular Scorn is a vengeful jailor spirit who is also imprisoned at the bottom of his Well along with a host of other prisoners. His art features scales and he's wearing a blindfold like the iconic image of Justice, but he also has a host of floating eyes around him and a big ol' enormous eye in his chest which indicates how he's subverting the "justice is blind" ideal. One of the Seekers available is Naz (she/her), a talented orc strategist with a big sword. Her tactical acumen is represented by being able to shuffle around progress tokens on challenges currently in play. The second Seeker is a lucky human bard named Feyn (he/him) who has a mysterious past, upbeat outlook, and a sweet lute. As is typical of bards in these party-based games, Feyn excels at supporting his teammates by granting re-rolls and has cards that can enable card draw. Drawing cards is always good in these kinds of games and becomes even more appreciated when you find out how difficult it is to normally refill your hand.

Callous's Lab, the third Kinfire Delve box set. Credit: Jake Bennington

The final of the trilogy is Callous' Lab. Callous is an immortal being afflicted by a malady that is slowly killing him, leaving him to wrestle with his newfound mortality through alchemical experimentations that he's more than willing to perform on the Seekers who come to stop him. Bundled in this box are Roland and Valora. Roland (he/him) is a dwarven scholar who is adept at fire magic. He is uniquely skilled at boosting his fellow Seekers' attempts at challenges, both because he can help them draw cards and because every single card in his deck is functionally a wild card for boosts meaning he doesn't have to match colors. He can also hit incredibly hard. Valora (she/her) is a runaway human noble-turned-archer who, by leveraging her bow, is adept at applying progress to multiple challenges and sports a few tools that can allow her to bypass a typically required roll of the dice.

The game is designed so that any of the Seekers can be played against any of the Well Masters. Mix and match between the sets to your heart's content!

Overview

An example of a game in progress. Credit: Jake Bennington

During the game, each player will take control of one of the Seekers mentioned above. This is represented by a card with your character's special passive ability, a lantern card that's essentially an enhanced attack that needs to be charged up during gameplay, and a deck of 18 cards that are each an attack that you can play to attempt a challenge. These challenges are found in the Well deck of 57 cards which serves double duty in that it not only holds the various encounters your Seekers will have to overcome, but it also serves as an indicator for how far your party has managed to delve. I quite enjoy this mechanic because a common reward of completing challenges is to delve a number of cards. Delving cards just means taking the top X cards of the Well deck and placing them into a face down pile off to the side which gets you ever closer to the boss residing at the bottom of the Well. It allows for more variation in each game since you'll be seeing different encounters based on the luck of the draw while still progressing through the whole deck.

On the subject of variation between games, each of the Well Masters actually has three different versions. Part of setup has you shuffling the three cards together and choosing one at random which resides face-down in the middle of the table. Even after becoming familiar with the game, there's no telling which iteration of the Master you're going to be up against so players are kept on their toes. Four Well cards are also dealt face up to surround the Master; these are the first four options a player has on each turn to try to defeat. As the challenges are defeated or discarded, another will take its place from the top of the deck. This process repeats until the Well deck runs dry. At this point, the Seekers have reached the bottom of the Well and proceed to fight the Master! I'll speak more on the Well Master fights later because they shake things up just enough to give a climactic end to a game.

A sample hand for Asha and a sample Well setup for delving into Vainglory's Grotto. Credit: Jake Bennington

Taking a look at the cards themselves, you'll notice that both the Seeker cards and the Well cards are divided up into three colors – blue, green, and red. A nice touch is that they each also have distinct shapes (square for blue, diamond for green, triangle for red) shown underneath the big number value in the top left corner which will allow anyone with color blindness still be able to discern between the three. Some Seeker cards can have two colors on them, which means you can treat them as either of the two colors shown. There are also a limited number of white Seeker cards (including all of the potent lanterns) which are functionally wild cards that can be played as either blue, green, or red depending on your needs at the time.

Gameplay

A turn follows a pretty simple structure that can be broken down into five steps.

First, the active player selects the challenge they want to attempt. This would be one of the four face-up cards surrounding the Well Master. The goal in attempting a challenge is to meet or beat the difficulty number in the top left of the card. Challenges each have a reward and penalty, shown on the card as the symbols next to the trophy and skull icons respectively. The reward is granted if the challenge is completed and the penalty is applied if it isn't. Even if the challenge is failed, a Seeker is typically putting some progress tokens on it which will make it easier to accomplish in the next turn. Most challenges have unique rules on them which makes it even more difficult to choose what to prioritize. Some even have bolded text which are effects that are in play even if you're attempting a different challenge.

Asha attempts the King's Ransom trap with the Defeat Trap card. There's even a boost from her teammate, Khor, represented by the card tucked up under Defeat Trap. Credit: Jake Bennington

Second, the player can choose a skill card from their hand (or their lantern if it is charged) and place it out on the board to show the other players. This skill card has to match the color of the challenge being attempted. Skill cards have a value that serves as your starting point for meeting the difficulty of the challenge, but most of them also have card text that gives them a variety of special rules and modifiers. This can range from ignoring penalties from failing the challenge, charging your Seeker's lantern, or allowing you to discard the card before attempting a challenge to gain some kind of powerful effect. It's worth mentioning that playing a skill card is optional in case a player wants to save their precious cards in hand and believes they can get by without spending one.

If the player does play a skill card, the next step is allowing the other Seekers to play their own cards as boosts. Boosting is achieved by looking at the bottom of a skill card. You'll see a little strip on the very bottom that contains the relevant color(s) and a value. When boosting, this is the only relevant part of a card – in fact, the booster can just slip it underneath the active player's skill card to make it even more obvious. Boosting can be done up to two times per skill card used, but it can only be done by other Seekers. Boosting your own cards isn't allowed. You also cannot boost if the player decides to not play a skill card in the previous step.

Not a particularly great roll here -- only one die face matches the color of the challenge, so Asha only gains +1 to her attempt. Fortunately, that's all they needed! Credit: Jake Bennington

Rolling the dice is the following step. There are four six-sided dice included in each box of Kinfire Delve. Three of the dice have two red, two blue, and two green faces each while the fourth has three white and three black results. After players have decided whether or not to boost, the active Seeker rolls all four dice. If any results come up that match the color of the challenge being attempted, they each add one to the Seeker's total. If the white face shows on that last die, it also counts as a success since white is wild. That might make you think the black result is bad and you'd be sort of right and sort of wrong. By itself, rolling the black result doesn't do anything. However, there are a variety of cards that can apply penalties if that result is rolled.

This Hunting Cat has some progress already on it from a previous attempt, meaning the next Seeker only needs to get 4 more to complete it. Credit: Jake Bennington

Finally, check to see if the challenge has been completed. You add up the value of the skill played, the value of any boosts applied, and the number of correct dice results rolled to get the total amount of progress that can be placed on the challenge this turn. If that amount meets or beats the difficulty of the challenge, great! It is completed and the active player gets the reward represented by the little trophy icon. The most common reward is delving some number of cards, but there are also fancier effects like drawing cards, charging your lantern, healing, or removing exhaustion. If the progress placed on the challenge doesn't get past its difficulty, the challenge is failed and the penalty next to the skull icon is applied. Often, this is damage suffered by the party, but just like the rewards, there are other unpleasant surprises awaiting on some cards. Things like forcing you to discard cards, ascend back up levels (putting previously delved cards back into the deck), or even attaching to the Seeker to cause negative effects for the rest of the game. Progress applied will stick around, though!

The end of the turn has some basic clean-up effects. Players take the cards they played this turn, either as skills or boosts, and put them in their discard piles. If there are any vacant slots surrounding the Well Master, they get refilled by the top card(s) of the Well deck. After that, play passes to the next Seeker and it all starts from the top.

Turns are pretty snappy in the game, so even with four player games I've never had to sit around impatiently waiting to take my turn again. The boost mechanic also provides for some interaction opportunities on other players' turns, and the cooperative nature of the game has always lead to discussions about who is planning what attack and how terrified we all were of some particularly nasty penalty.

Fighting the Well Master

Vainglory is surrounded by her Gauntlet cards. Players can't begin progress on Vainglory until at least one of these gauntlets have been defeated. Normally, Vainglory would have flipped here but I didn't want to ruin the surprise for anyone's first encounters with her! Credit: Jake Bennington

If at any point you need to draw a card from the Well deck but there aren't any, you've reached the bottom and are ready to fight the Well Master. All the remaining challenges are removed, the face-down Master card is flipped over, and the four gauntlet cards set aside at the beginning of the game are laid out around the Master. These gauntlet cards are tricky challenges that bar the way from attacking the Master until they're dealt with. In fact, the Well Master card is always a black challenge and not one of the colors associated with cards. This means it's impossible to pick a matching skill from your hand to attempt them (since even the white skills are really just treated as red, blue, or green). Defeating the gauntlet cards here will flip them face-down instead of removing them, and the back sides of most of these have rules as well. In most cases, you will unlock a vulnerability to that color to go after the Master. For instance, defeating the red Reprisal card from Scorn will allow all the Seekers to start attacking Scorn with red skill cards.

The Well Master fight follows all the normal flow of the rest of the game, but adding the gauntlet cards and the unique effect of whichever form of the Master was randomly chosen makes it just different enough to feel the shift. It reminds me of the mentality of a video game where you hear the boss music kick in right before a tough fight. The penalties start to really ramp up which means that one way or another, the game is going to come to a close pretty shortly after reaching the bottom of the Well.

Perils of Delving

The Exhausted deck is full of nasty surprises for the party who also has to contend with a shared health pool that only goes up to 10. Credit: Jake Bennington

Eagle-eyed readers may have noted that at no point did I mention drawing new cards in a turn. That's because unlike many other games, you don't refill your hand at the beginning or end of your turn. Card draw is an effect available from a few sources, but it's quite rare. Instead, if a Seeker wants more cards, they have to engage with the exhaustion mechanic. At the start of a player's turn, they can discard the remaining cards in their hand to draw a new hand or if they have no cards in hand, they must draw a new hand. Each time this is done, one of the exhausted cards is flipped up, the player draws their hand of cards, and then takes their turn as normal. Each of the Well Masters have a unique deck of six exhausted cards and they're genuinely all terrible. They include effects like "each time you suffer a damage, suffer another damage" or "if you have three copies of this card in play, lose the game" or "if a player plays a certain card name, lose the game." There's a lot of "lose the game" involved there, so managing exhaustion is pretty important.

Taking damage has also been mentioned a few times and it's another route to losing the game. At the start of the game, the party has 10 health. Yes, it's the party as a whole. Health is a shared resource and there's only 10 of it. While healing and damage reduction effects do exist, they're not exactly plentiful and in my dozen or so games I have almost always felt like we were in danger of running out at some point.

At this point, I've won more games than I have lost, but I've still definitely lost my fair share. I enjoy that it's not a guarantee to win the game every time you sit down so there's always some tension present. It also feels like some of the Well Masters are easier (e.g. Vainglory has become my go-to for teaching the game) and I'm sure some of the Seekers are more potent than others. Synergy among the Seekers is also lurking, with potential combos like Valora spreading progress around multiple challenges which then enables Naz to shift it onto a primary target. This means there are plenty of dials for the players to adjust to get the game to their desired challenge level. The rulebook does also offer a "hard mode" but all that entails is starting at 8 health instead of 10, which I guess does achieve the desired result but it feels a little bland given how much character and pizazz the rest of the game offers.

Final Thoughts

I'm one of those people who has a board game shelf with a few dozen various games, some of which I am embarrassed to say I've owned for years and still haven't played. Kinfire Delve definitely isn't one of those games languishing on the shelf. My wife and I have played it many times, I have taken it with me to conventions and tournaments to play after rounds, and we have shared it with my wife's D&D group who took to it with ease and enthusiasm. It's portable, teaches and plays fast, is relatively affordable for what can be an expensive hobby, and is just a genuinely solid game that I have to give it my endorsement. If you think it sounds remotely interesting, I suggest you give it a try!

title: Competitive Innovations in the Mortal Realms: 2026-08-19
content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Thoughts

Both lists utilize Be'lakor as their leader, but change the composition. List 1 goes for a more elite, with a big brick of Chosen alongside the Warriors and Knights. This is the list to take if your opponent doesn't have a ton of stuff on the other side and you need something to hit real hard, to crack an opponent with an iron shell.

Thoughts

Within 1 faction, these lists couldn't play any more differently. The Severith list is very mobile, with Windchargers and Severith they can dart around the board, plink away at enemies from safety before charging in for the kill. Thoughts

Cities of Sigmar are in a really strong position to handle Sylvaneth, especially post-Sylvaneth nerf. Sylvaneth generally try and play cagey, creating denial zones the enemy doesn't want to tread (And slowly expanding this across the board) while Cities castles up, charging only if it has to.

This puts Sylvaneth in a position where their usual strike and fade tactics don't work. If they're charged, Cavaliers will simply charge out of combat. While they can't leave combat, they can position themselves so it's very difficult to maximize damage against them. This leaves Sylvaneth stranded and easy to be picked apart.

This is pretty much the platonic ideal for Cities of Sigmar right now. Cavaliers want to be charged, if the enemy charges them the Steelhelms pull all the attacks onto them and the Cavaliers can charge even in combat, meaning their damage isn't blunted by being charged. Even better if there's a better target to pick on nearby.

If they aren't charged, they can still take the initiative. That's fine. Supporting them is shooting units like the Fusiliers and Tahlia who can lead from the front with some nasty damage output and support.

title: Disney Lorcana's new online game could dominate 2027, but only if it moves fast
content:
The big reveal at Ravensburger's D23 panel last weekend was that a digital version of Disney Lorcana is officially "in the works". If I had to guess what that means, I'd suppose it'll be out some time in 2027. Any longer and it seems an odd time to reveal it, any shorter and we'd expect to also see a release date. Whenever it gets here, an official, digital client for Disney Lorcana is likely to be absolutely huge for the TCG, and I'm now thinking that the card game's fourth year could be its biggest yet.

A digital platform for Lorcana has the potential to make the game accessible to thousands of Disney fans who might never have had the motivation or opportunity to pick up card packs, build a deck, and find an in-person game. Its arrival could be just the shot in the arm Lorcana needs to keep it from slumping.

The TCG market is tricky to break into and only a tiny fraction of the games that get started find proper success. Lorcana has already done very well for itself, of course, helped in no small part by its attachment to Disney. But after its first couple of years, and a record-breaking 2024 for creator Ravensburger, it did seem like the game might have peaked. 

In January 2026, the company revealed that it had suffered a 5.9% decline, and that its TCG had shrunk over 2025. It chalked this up to the investment crowd pulling out, which to an extent matches what we've observed - as all of the most expensive Disney Lorcana card sales took place in the first year of its release.

The benefits of a digital release are obvious. Chiefly, it will widen Lorcana's reach and get more people involved in the game - especially since Ravensburger plans to bring it to mobile as well as PC. There will be way, way more people willing to give Lorcana a try like this - when the computer does all the rules tracking for you and you don't have to go out and talk to (shudder) other people.

The digital version can then serve as an on-ramp to the physical game. It's a tried and true method that has worked before. I don't know if I personally would have ever tried Magic: The Gathering if I hadn't got in on the ground floor of Arena, and now I'm a tabletop writer and go to Commander nights most weeks.

Perhaps a little less wholesome, it also gives Lorcana a new, digital economy, one that Ravensburger can retain total control over. We'll hope, of course, that Lorcana Online is generous with its F2P content, but either way, its creator has the potential to make a killing from in-game purchases.

There are some downsides to going digital too. Without proper care, a digital version can start to cannibalize a physical TCG and fragment its playerbase. 

But the upsides are high, and Ravensburger needs to get its game out as fast as possible, without rushing it and turning in a buggy mess of course. I really think it needs to have the game out next year. Lorcana shrank in 2025. If that pattern continues, and if we have to wait until 2029 for the release, it might be too late for the physical game when it does finally hit.

And, not to be mean, but some individuals have managed to make unofficial versions of a Lorcana client already, turning out smoothly running websites very quickly. Surely with its extra resources, Ravensburger can do likewise?

title: Spirit Train is an utterly gorgeous Ghibli-inspired board game, so why doesn't it entice me?
content:
It's tough to be original in any medium, let alone board games. Our art form has taken off far later than the likes of film, television, and digital gaming. With so many centuries of storytelling to draw from, intentionally or not, it's tough to say we're ever first to anything. Still, it's nice to nod to the shoulders we stand on. Spirit Train, a new board game that recently hit Kickstarter, does not appear to do so.

This breathtakingly gorgeous board game ticks all the boxes for a trendy crowdfunding hit. Firstly, its vibes are overwhelmingly cozy. You play a psychopomp who wants to score the most points by ferrying cutesy characters to their preferred version of the afterlife.

Your train and its cargo are realized through lovingly-crafted Ghibli-esque art, found on every page, component, and spare scrap of space. Players even get to place tetromino-style pieces into a 3D spirit train that (because this is crowdfunding) is exclusive to Kickstarter backers. In a word, it's stunning. What's not to love?

I don't love that this is just Spiritfarer: The Board Game. For the unfamiliar, Spiritfarer is a beloved indie videogame from 2020 that's about - you guessed it - ferrying adorable critters to their intended afterlife. It's a gentle yet extremely affecting story about accepting death as part of life. It was the first cozy game to make me cry, and that experience sticks with me, years later.

Spiritfarer takes place on a ship (that, fun fact, was originally going to be a train), and it's slightly less Ghibli in its art style, but that's about where the differences end. And all I'm saying is: some credit would have been classy.

It's possible that Spirit Train creators SweaterBear Games have never heard of SpiritFarer. If so, I apologize for all the complaints of copying. But the concepts are just so damn similar. It seems impossible that one can exist without knowing about the other. It looks like an egregious case of 'copy their homework, but change a few of the words.'

For many, that won't be a problem. I bet there are plenty of Spiritfarer fans who actually welcome a similar experience, only in tabletop form. It's just the lack of credit that leaves a bad taste in my mouth. It's common for board games to wear their inspirations on their sleeves (in fact, it's often a popular marketing tactic), so why not here?

I won't be backing this one, but I'm keen to see how Spirit Train turns out regardless. Nothing would shut my moaning mouth harder than seeing this game turn out brilliant. I hope it does - because I don't ever wish for somebody's passion project to fail, and because people have already spent $173,000 backing this thing.

SweaterBear Games has three previous board games under its belt. All are known for their phenomenal production value, and they've received very positive reviews. The most common critique across the board is that these games can be a little too fiddly.

Spirit Train has a 36-page (first draft) rulebook for a game that lasts 90 minutes, and most of the Kickstarter page is taken up advertising its lush components. That reputation for fiddliness might continue, but it's hard to know without actually playing.

What we do know is you earn points by interacting with spirits on your train, helping them reach the afterlife, and collecting 'spirit stones'. Each round, you'll collect tickets, move your train across the map, and draw interaction cards to mingle with passengers. Then, you'll upgrade the spirits on your train, and manage which spirits are staying for the long haul or getting off at the next stop.

That's a simplification that doesn't cover the event cards that shape your game at the start of every round. Nor does it mention the secret train-building mechanic that decides what rooms (and actions) are available to you each day. There's a lot of moving parts to this one (as you'd expect from a locomotive).

It gives you the general gist, however. That, combined with more details found on the Kickstarter page, should help you decide whether this is a train you want to ride - or whether you'd rather walk.

Want to share your own opinions on the best board games around? Hit us up in the Wargamer Discord.

title: BattleTech Mech Overview: Firestarter
content:
Welcome back, MechWarriors! Lynn's here today to talk about a mech which could be deemed a Prodigy of external combustion, a true threat to enemy logistics, more than capable of burning off The Fat of the Land.

That's right, it's the Firestarter. The twisted, 35 ton Firestarter.

Firestarter. Credit: porble

Well, I say the Firestarter is a 35-tonner... The BattleMech is, but this is one of the mechs with an OmniMech sister chassis, and the Omni Firestarter, despite sharing the same model number prefix and being classed as a variant of the same chassis on the (current) Master Unit List, is a full ten tons heavier. I plan to cover both versions today, since the voices won't let me be if I'm not comprehensive in my approach.

Before we get properly (Fire)started, I want to speak a bit about the role of the humble flamer in mech combat. The basic Flamer is Infantry Guy's dream, delivering a whopping 4d6 damage to conventional infantry (better than a heavy machine gun!), but against other targets it is… significantly less impressive. Unlike Inferno SRMs and Plasma weapons, the Flamer has no special enhanced effect on vehicles or battle armor, as far as I'm aware. And against mechs, well…

A traditional Inner Sphere Flamer weighs a full ton, has the range bands of a basic Small Laser, and generates 3 heat for the firing mech. In exchange, Flamers have historically inflicted either 2 (direct energy) damage or 2 points of heat to a target mech, firer’s choice. I’m not aware of any fluff justification for the “dealer’s choice” aspect; I could imagine that the focus of the plasma jet can be dialed between “cutting torch” and “diffuse flame” modes, but TechManual gave no explanation (spending most of the Flamer 's page space simply talking about how it kind of sucks in mech combat).

Fortunately for the Firestarter, the mech most closely tied to the Flamer, the new Core Rules have increased the utility of the Flamer… somewhat. Flamers now deal both their physical and heat damage to the target, placing them on the “Plasma Rifle” side of the heat-inflicting weapons divide (with Inferno SRMs and Plasma Cannons still on the “heat only” side). Perhaps more importantly, Fire/Smoke environmental rules have been massively simplified in Core, AND heat damage from non-SRM sources is more efficient at setting flammable hexes (mostly woods and buildings) on fire than Inferno missiles are, only requiring four points of heat damage, or two regular Flamers, rather than four missiles.

Notably, being inside a hex on fire at the start of the Heat Phase inflicts 5 extra heat on a mech, and a hex targeted by heat damage catches on fire at the end of the Weapons Phase! Combined with hexes being significantly easier to hit than mechs, as immobile targets, this means that two Flamers are now a pretty dang efficient way to inconvenience the infamous Assault Mech On A Hill In Heavy Woods, particularly the barely-heat-neutral crowd like the Hellstar and the Awesome 11H.

It may not surprise you to hear that MOST Firestarters mount 2+ Flamers.

With that in mind, let's see how the Firestarter fares against our grading scale in the brave new world of the 2026 Core Rules!

Variants

These mechs have all been reviewed based on a standard F through S scale, which you can find described on our landing page here (along with all of our other ‘Mech reviews, the name of the box you can buy to get any of the mechs we have covered, and our general methodology).

4th Sword of Light FS9-A Firestarter. Credit: Valk.

FS9-A

The original-model Firestarter, this is a variant that didn't last long, introduced in 2550 and extinct by the Late Succession Wars. The most persistent Firestarter feature it introduced was its movement profile, with all but two models moving at the same 6/9/6 speed, regardless of the tech involved in getting them there. The FS9-A pairs this with an 87% armor load, notably AC/10-proof on all (non-head, natch) front-facing locations, and IS ML-proof across the back. For weapons, its base 10 single heat sinks are taxed by, uh, one front-facing and one rear-facing flamer in the CT (probably the second-most common trait among Firestarters), a medium laser and a flamer in each arm, and a small laser in each side torso.

For those keeping track at home, that means the FS9-A would go to +9 heat on a running alpha strike with its front-facing weapons, so don't do that. Fortunately, it isn't really meant to do that. Against hard targets, all the lasers are heat-neutral at a run, and you can juggle a good spread of reasonable alternate firing patterns depending on the range and your needs at the time: all the Range 1/2/3 weapons, for instance, build 1+movement and threaten 12 damage and 6 heat. Those numbers won't, ah, set the world on fire, but the 9-A is okay as a mid-speed IntroTech 35-tonner. Just try to use terrain to your advantage for screening on the way in, since the longest-range weapons this thing has are bog-standard medium lasers, and with its armor + TMM combo it won't survive significant attention from an enemy.

Still, at 773 BV, cheapness has a quality all its own, and if you want a dork to run around torching woods, this lil guy sure will do that!

Lynn's Rating: C.

FS9-B

Oh. I see how it is.

So, the "iconic" Firestarter, the second variant introduced in the timeline, is the FS9-H, but earlier letters got introduced out of sequence, sure, whatever. I can deal with this.

We've gone from the Star League to the Jihad with this one, because B Is For Blakist. This little weirdo uses an endo steel frame, light ferro-fibrous armor, and a light fusion engine, but doesn't put the weight where you might expect. The armor is thinner than the A (which is a common trend, I'm sad to say), and the weapons are down to the traditional front-rear CT flamers, a flamer in the left arm, and an ER Medium Laser in the right arm. The B is still at a base 10 heat sinks, and yeah, they're still singles, and yeah, it still overheats if it fires all its forward-facing weapons at once.

So what has actually been improved on the FS9-B, rather than just enshittified? Well, the movement profile jumps up to 6/9/8 via Improved Jump Jets, and this lil guy carries C3i. This oddball package will set you back 668 BV.

So, Hear Me Out. This mech is dogwater at any form of conventional combat, but that doesn't mean it isn't useful. This is a very cheap way to get a Jump 8 C3i spotter on the field, and the flamers can be used for fun (setting hexes on fire) and activities (setting people on fire). That's actually a good amount of utility for the Blakist on a budget, so if you want to twirl your cybernetically-enhanced moustache on the cheap, give this option some thought. Just remember that if you're shooting at anything that can effectively shoot back, you aren't villaining right.

Lynn's Rating: C+, as long as you can embrace the bastard within.

FS9-C

C is for... Circinus Federation? Sure, okay. We have Ferro-Fibrous armor this time (82% coverage, lighter than the A but heavier than the B, distributed to be significantly thinner on the limbs than the torso), and a standard-engine-powered 6/9/6 profile. The arms each mount the ol' standard ML + Flamer, but the torso weapons... ahh, the torso weapons...

This is the Obligatory Periphery Rocket Launcher Variant, mounting four 10s and two 15s for a total of 70 tubes. Shockingly for a rocket mech, it only builds movement heat if it presses the "ALL ZE ROCKETS" button.

Honestly, if this wasn't 940 BV I'd say it's kind of cooking, but I don't rate a single unreliable burst of damage that highly. Excellent shitty pirate NPC mech to throw at players in a narrative scenario, though, and when it does manage to punch up it'll be so funny.

Lynn's Rating: D+, but a very fun D+

FS9-H

I was expecting to find out that H was for "Hegemony" or something, but I think the true meaning of this H is "this mech was introduced before FASA established any real pattern to model numbers, and someone just thought it sounded cool"; this base model of the Firestarter was originally built on Skye.

This is an FS9-A but with the side torso small lasers replaced with machine guns. The full ton of machine gun ammo in the right torso necessitates dropping a ton of armor, with the arms, in particular, dropping down to a Ostmech-thin coat of 6 armor pips.

Compared to the FS9-A, the -H model is only better at killing even larger numbers of conventional infantry (or, you know, civilians). The SLs were not the source of the -A's heat issues, and when fighting hard targets the -H puts out less damage, can absorb less damage, and can now explode. The fact that the -H still became manufacturer Argile Technologies' most successful model of Firestarter should tell you something about what most buyers were using Firestarters to do.

At least Infantry Guy's Warcrime Machine only runs 694 BV?

Lynn's Rating: D.

FS9-HB

This one isn't even real! From the world of BattleTech Gothic, the HB is an H which drops the MGs and ammo, swaps the MLs for Light Blazers, and adds one (1) heat sink. This arguably has some utility even outside the world of Gothic (where the Light Blazers' "Dazzle Mode" gives benefits against monstrous Abominations), since the Light Blazers give it a pair of 7 damage hits and only build 1+movement heat if you can keep your fingers off the flamer triggers, but it's up to 754 BV and, again, doesn't exist in canon.

Lynn's Rating: IDEK, y'all.

Battletech Gothic Firestarter. Credit: Jack Hunter

FS9-K

K is for... Kapellan? Something is off here.

Anyway, this is a weirdo Star-League-Era Capellan variant, an H which drops all the regular armaments out of the arms and side torsos in order to mount two SLs in the left arm and a large laser in the right arm. This allows the K to either (fairly gently) poke opponents from medium range or fire all the lasers at movement heat when it gets in close to... deal the same damage as the H's MLs + MGs, in a different arrangement of clusters. The single forward-mounting and single rear-mounting flamer in its CT feel mostly vestigial, but could still hypothetically come in clutch if you need to throw off a TSM mech's math, I suppose.

At least it can't explode?

Lynn's Rating: D-.

FS9-M 'Mirage'

Here it is, the one Firestarter which dared to be different. The "Mirage" is the only mech bearing the Firestarter name to mount zero Flamers. And it was only in production for a single year before the factory was destroyed, and no subsequent manufacturer ever picked it back up. Oh, there are more FS9-Ms, there's even a "Mirage II," but they all mount flamers. Even the OmniMech variant hard-mounts the traditional CT flamers to ensure this would never happen again!

Like the Skye Rangers (who maintained a lance of Mirages with one arm painted black in memoriam after the battle which destroyed the factory), I am still in mourning over this, because this is a pretty damn decent 35-tonner. The Mirage steps up to a full coat of armor, rearranges the jump jets and heat sinks relative to normal Firestarters (and picks up an 11th heat sink it really doesn't need), and pairs the H's side torso machine guns with a medium laser and a small laser in each arm.

This guy is chunky enough to take a hit, can deal a PSR's worth of damage to enemy mechs (a rarity among Firestarters!), and with the MGs it can still kill the perfidious infantryman every now and then, as a treat. What it can't do is set fires, however, which I'll admit does make it look worse in the Core Rules future to come than it did a couple months ago.

Still, 798 BV for a lil guy who can actually scrap with other mechs (albeit at prohibitively short range) isn't so bad.

Lynn's Rating: C.

FS9-M2

Like Tenacious D's classic "Tribute," the FS9-M2 doesn't sound anything like that song the FS9-M. A widespread Late Republic era variant, based on the MechWarrior Dark Age ("ClickyTech") Firestarter, the M2 utilizes endo steel structure and double heat sinks to allow it to pair fairly thick armor (94% coverage) with six Flamers, three in each arm, plus a single head-mounted ER Medium Laser, while only building 1+movement heat on an alpha strike.

The inefficiency of Flamers at heating up enemy mechs means you still can't quite hit the +15 external heat threshold with this mech, but you could multi-target to set three woods hexes on fire in the same turn, which could be both extremely funny and genuinely useful. And this is still south of 800 BV, at 751!

Am I grading Firestarters on a curve? Maybe, but on that curve this thing really isn't bad.

Lynn's Rating: C+.

FS9-M3

Huh. Those are some choices. The M3 is an M2 which drops all the left arm flamers and the eleventh double heat sink in order to max the armor back out (in the same configuration as the original M), add a TAG module to the right torso, add a small laser in the left arm, and pick up MASC, without dropping the JJs, for a BV-inflating 6/9(12)/6 movement profile.

Honestly, I dislike this less than I thought I would when I saw the MASC? Its anti-mech damage is back down to "FS9-H lasers and machine guns" levels, and its BV is up to 866, but the MASC is genuinely helpful for getting the M3 to the right places for its flamers and/or TAG to matter, and the new Core Rules (and, more broadly, missions with objectives) do have a place for pure utility pieces like this when they're cheap enough. Kinda wish it could've packed in an Active Probe, or hands (almost no Firestarters have hands!), if it's going to be living the objective dork life, but... yeah, you could do worse with this BV for an objective dork.

Lynn's Rating: C?

FS9-M4

I'm pretty sure I own the exact MWDA sculpt which gave us this record sheet.

The M4 is an M2 which swaps to an XL engine and drops the ERML, the left arm flamers, and the 11th heat sink in exchange for the full armor coat and a RAC/2 with a single ton of ammo. This is... okay, I guess? The RAC/2 lets it spin to win trying to critseek opponents downrange while it runs around doing objectives and setting hexes on fire, and it can weather a little return fire, though even with new ammo explosion rules that (well-padded, at least) ammo crit slot will kill the mech if hit. It's still really dang cheap at 798 BV, and can do something at ranges few Firestarters can, but it doesn't spark joy in me.

Lynn's Rating: C-.

Found it! Dragon's Fury Veteran Firestarter, from MechWarrior: Dark Age's Fire For Effect Expansion. Photo Credit: Lynn B.

FS9-N 'Mirage II'

Oh god, there's a lot going on here. And this still has nothing to do with the original Mirage! What's with all these weird modern sequels?

A spiritual successor to the troubled experimental FS9-X81 model (we'll get there), this Dark Age variant from the Recognition Guides brings in a buttload of advanced tech. We've got... Inner Sphere Endo-Composite, eleven IS Double Heat Sinks, a full coat of Reflective Armor, a Clan-spec XL engine, and a weapons load like an FS9-A on PCP: A Clan ERML and an IS Flamer in each arm, Clan ERSLs in each side torso, and the ubiquitous rear-facing CT flamer paired with a front-facing Sea-Fox-supplied Plasma Cannon (with one ton of ammo in the right torso). In proper FS9-A tradition, the Mirage II does not want to hit the big red button, but the long(-er) range weapons are heat negative at a run, and all the front-facing weapons except the plasma cannon work out to be neutral at a run.

There's significantly higher damage potential here than most Firestarters, plus higher heat-generation capability than most, plus situationally excellent durability, but you sure do pay for it. At a princely 1,660 BV, higher than all but one other Firestarter (the OR variant of the 45-ton OmniMech, also equipped with Clan tech), this is too rich for my blood. A little birdie has hinted to me that Reflective Armor BV is coming down a bit in the upcoming BV 2.5, to account for the increased vulnerabilities it brings to physical attacks and falls, and it's plausible that the very high BV of plasma cannons could drop at the same time, but that's a whole lot of maybes that would have to become definitelys before I would seriously consider fielding this mech.

Lynn's Rating: D, but an "Awesome But Impractical" D.

FS9-P

A Civil-War-era Periphery variant, the P mysteriously does not use the same chassis as the C, instead pairing an endo steel skeleton with standard armor in a differently thin coat, gaining one pip on the arms relative to the H in exchange for losing pips on the legs, side torsos, and all rear torso locations. The arms each carry a medium laser and a flamer, in the grand tradition of yore, but the P's armament differs from there, with a front-facing flamer, small laser, and SRM 2 in each side torso, with the single ton of SRM 2 ammo nestled in the CT. An alpha strike would build 4+movement heat, hot but plausible in the right circumstances, and this does have excellent damage output for 775 BV, but, uh... sure is a shame about that (lack of) armor. When an Inner Sphere Large Laser goes internal on any limb, and you're still moving 6/9/6, I don't have high hopes for your life expectancy.

Lynn's Rating: D+.

FS9-S

Okay, the S series are the "Doin' Stuff with LosTech" series of Firestarters, with the S and S1 dating from the very-late-Renaissance/very-early-Clan-Invasion period and the S2 and S3 popping up amidst the Jihad.

The S has an endo steel structure, the classic arm weapons and CT flamers, a small laser in the RT, and both an AMS with one ton of ammo and a Beagle Active Probe in the LT. It's still on ten singles for heat sinks, and it manages to find yet another novel arrangement of armor pips, with the same thin coat as the P on its front-facing locations, but noticeably thicker rear armor, IS-MPL-proof across the back.

It's 754 BV. It's cheap but flimsy. The Active Probe is the only real distinguishing feature it has.

Lynn's Rating: D.

FS9-S1

It's an S but with an ECM instead of the Active Probe. That's it, that's the only change, and it's up to 820 BV.

Lynn's Rating: D-.

FS9-S2

Okay, this one is on the same skeleton, with the same armor load, as the -B, but with a standard engine instead of the light, and double heat sinks. Weapons and equipment are almost the same as the -S, but the arm lasers are ERMLs. It's 842 BV.

I do like a Firestarter that can think about alpha striking, but this armor load is not a good layout, and this is less mobile and has more of its utility wrapped up in its actual damage output than the B does.

Lynn's Rating: D+.

FS9-S3

This is the ECM variant of the S2, same as the S1 for the S. 908 BV.

Lynn's Rating: D.

Firestarter. Credit: Rockfish

FS9-X81

The wacky Unique experimental Firestarter which does everything wrong, the X81 pairs the H's armor load with ten double heat sinks and an XXL engine (still at the same 210 rating, still 6/9/6) so that it can mount the traditional CT flamers, a flamer and an Medium X-Pulse Laser in the left arm, and a Plasma Rifle (with one ton of ammo) and an MXPL in the right arm.

A Firestarter with a Plasma Rifle sounds like great fun, but this is not the right way to get there. Terrible armor, even-more-terrible heat management, 1,065 BV... there's good reason why this one is considered a failed prototype in-universe.

Lynn's Rating: F.

Conclusions

The Firestarter certainly brings value to the battlefield, and the Core Rules enhance that value, but that value does not really lie in fighting mechs. The best Firestarters, in my opinion, are the ones that are cheap, reasonably durable, and outfitted for Activities more than direct combat. The A, the M2, the B if you're nasty, the M3 if you've got the points. An EWAR suite would seem in keeping with this purpose, and I wish I liked the S series more, but their armor is bad, y'all, and they can't play keep-away as easily as the B.

Whew! Okay, that's all the Firestarters! Thanks for reading, hope you enjoyed, see you...

...dammit. Right. The voices demand I talk about the 45-ton Omni Firestarter. sigh

Hastati Sentinels Firestarter. Credit: Jack Hunter

The Other Firestarter

One of the earliest and most widespread Inner Sphere OmniMechs, the Omni Firestarter came to be as the result of passive-aggressive pettiness between Lyran manufacturer Coventry Metal Works and Combine manufacturer Luthien Armor Works in the early stages of the shaky technology-sharing agreements forged between their nations in response to the Clan Invasion, as each of them tried to share the least-advantageous specs they could with their rivals. Fortunately for us, from a BV-balanced perspective, I'd say their attempts at sabotage failed; this is a pretty dang solid budget trooper medium mech.

The basic body of the Omni Firestarter is an enlarged 45-ton chassis with an endo steel frame, an XL engine, and a pretty good coat of standard armor, if a little light on the legs: 12 pips on the arms, 16 on the legs and front-facing side torsos, 20 CT, the full 9 head, and 6/7/6 across the back. It gives itself design constraints by forcing some aspects of the Firestarter identity on all configurations: it fixes a full load of 6 jump jets to guarantee the 6/9/6 movement profile, fixes the traditional front and rear facing CT flamers, and fixes two additional double heat sinks (which are not hidden in the engine on the crit chart)... that's seven tons sunk into fixed equipment, and only 13.5 tons of pod space.

The good news for the mech's utility in BV-balanced gaming is that none of that fixed equipment is particularly expensive (the naked frame only costs 646 BV!), and with the critical slot constraints of the endo steel and the XL engine on top of all of that, the FS9-O really doesn't have enough rope to hang itself with overpriced loadouts (mostly). The only real tragedy is that in the Core Rules, the fixed single flamers to the front and rear aren't enough to set woods on fire without assistance, and there is a grand total of one Omni-config which mounts additional flamers.

Yeah, that's right, I'm describing a lack of flamers as a tragedy. What is this strange new world in which we live?

Still, while the Omni Firestarter isn't particularly good at starting fires, it's actually surprisingly good at the whole "mech combat" thing. Let's take a closer look!

FS9-O

The "Prime" configuration here is the one Omnistarter which embraces the notion of "What if Firestarter, but big?" It slaps a large laser in each arm, two additional flamers in the right arm, and a Beagle Active Probe in the RT. The front-facing weapons build 1+ movement heat, and this runs 1,144 BV.

This feels just a hair pricey for what it is, but this is decent damage, decent mobility, good durability, and can torch woods if that's helpful. Not bad!

Lynn's Rating: C.

FS9-OA

LB 10-X. Two tons of ammo. Small laser thanks to that last half ton of pod space. That's it. 976 BV.

This isn't quite the Minimum Viable LB 10 in the game, but it's pretty dang close. I think LB 10-Xs are fantastic weapons, and even though this mech can't force a PSR on its own, it has a very clear role to play as a premiere inhabitant of Liberty's "Little Bastard" zone. That said, the Arctic Fox AF1B is arguably even better value if you just want a cheapass Omni with a Golden BB gun, and lives on some of the same availability lists.

Lynn's Rating: C+.

FS9-OB

Pulse spam on a budget. The OB mounts an LPL, two MPLs, a TAG, a C3S, and a Small Laser, for 1,070 BV. I'm actually going to say the C3S is the secret sauce here. While C3 is a very difficult tool to use well, extending the range at which Inner Sphere MPLs can exercise their pulse bonus is one of its more useful applications, and the new Core Rules guarantee you can get some value from a network even in the face of enemy ECM.

Even outside of a network, a PSR's worth of pulse lasers on a decently mobile, decently durable chassis makes for a pretty good rat-hunter to keep the flimsier striker lights off more valuable mechs' backs.

Lynn's Rating: B.

FS9-OC

This... is one of those mechs that's more useful in scenarios outside the average pickup or tournament game. Mounting two LRM 10s with two tons of ammo, a small laser, and a C3S for 1,006 BV, this is basically a funny-looking Whitworth. It's not entirely Whitworthless, though; 10 is, amusingly, the smallest sized launcher which can deploy a minefield with Core Rules Thunder LRMs, and I suppose it's cheap enough to make for a funny backline pest in a C3 network, particularly since ECM bubbles are six hexes and the short range of LRMs is seven; a spotter can sit just outside ECM radius and deliver full benefit.

That said, it's still not optimal, particularly given that its two tons of ammunition constrict its access to specialty ammo somewhat.

Lynn's Rating: D+, maaaaybe up to a C- in a C3 network.

FS9-OD

*squints* Is that a... Vindicator? Huh.

ERPPC, LRM 5 with one ton of ammo, medium laser, C3S, Guardian ECM, 1,322 BV.

That's alright? It's a little expensive for its output, and you can either get actual Vindicators to be Vindicators for you for less BV (albeit at a slower speed), or, if you're Capellan, you could pay just a little more for a Vindy 7L and get a headcapping CERPPC and the enhanced durability of Reinforced Structure, but the ECM is handy (and only found on more-expensive stealth Vindicators). If you want a 6/9/6 Vindicator with an ECM suite, knock yourself out, I guess?

Lynn's Rating: C-.

FS9-OE

Oh hello there, Draconis Combine! The OE mounts up a Coordinator-approved weapons load of an MRM 20, MPL, SPL, and a sword for 998 BV. Sadly, they forgot the C3S on this one; the MRM could really benefit from a network, even in the new Core Rules. That said, this is a surprisingly good loadout? A six damage sword is unexciting, but with the new rules' mild debuff to kicking, you might actually use it sometimes, the shooting output is actually pretty good with the MRM buffs, and unlike some MRM mechs, this has absolutely no heat problems. You're not bad, OE.

Lynn's Rating: C+, though when BV 2.5 readdresses MRM BV this will probably drop to a plain C.

FS9-OF

I guess it makes sense that the "OF" is the hottest of the Omnistarters. That said, Mekbay's "Total Heat (Dissipation)" read of 42 (26) is misleading; this is actually a perfectly cohesive bracket-firing mech, if not the most exciting one. We have two ERLLs, two ERMLs, an ERSL, and one extra heat sink here. This means that running and firing both ERLLs is neutral, and running and firing one ERLL alongside the short-range lasers is neutral. That's okay damage, though it doesn't crest the "can inflict a PSR" threshold until the ERSL comes into play, and the range is significantly better than most Firestarters. It's 1,446 BV, though, and you can do better for that price.

Lynn's Rating: C-.

FS9-OG

The real OG is both boring and kind of at odds with itself, I'm afraid. It mounts an LB 5-X with two tons of ammo for long-range plinking and aircraft-bothering, paired with a trio of standard medium lasers. It has the heat sinking for ERMLs, but it doesn't use them, introducing the problem that an LB 5 enters its minimum range at three hexes, exactly when the MLs enter short, causing issues with accuracy and reliability for this mech's damage no matter where it stands. 1,063 BV is cheap, but I can't really imagine ever reaching for this thing when there's so many cooler toys on the shelf.

Lynn's Rating: D.

FS9-OH

...wow, there's a lot going on here. The OH utilizes every single open critical slot on the FS9-O frame! Let me slow down and unpack this. We've got an MPL, SPL, and two MGs in the left arm; an ERML in the LT; an AMS in the head; a half ton of MG ammo, single ton of AMS ammo, and CASE in the RT (and that CASE actually means something outside of campaign play now, with the new ammo explosion rules!); and an MPL, SPL, Beagle Active Probe, and Guardian ECM in the right arm. 1,119 BV.

I actually like this a lot? It builds movement heat on an alpha strike (or movement +1 if the AMS triggers twice), but that would include the rear flamer, so effectively it's usually heat neutral-to-negative. It has Firestarter-typical range issues which the lone ERML does nothing to really mitigate, but when it does get close it dumps damage in a way very few Firestarters can, making it a true striker mech, and the EWAR suite is useful in the new missions.

I think this isn't "good for a Firestarter," this is just a good mech. Huh.

Lynn's Rating: B+.

FS9-OR

Hey boss, we looted these Clan OmniPods, what should we do with them?

As with most-if-not-all "R" variants, this is "the MixTech one." Here the podspace is filled by two CERLLs and a CLRM 10 with Artemis IV and two tons of ammo. That is a significant long-range punch, in theory, but the heat curve isn't great here. The ERLLs alone build movement heat, and the LRM would add another 4 on top of that... You could hypothetically rotate between "all the long-range weapons" and "one ERLL and the LRM" on alternating turns; you'd never get to the to-hit penalties from heat, but you would slow to 5/8/6 during your cool-down turns. For 1,713 BV? That ain't worth the hassle.

Lynn's Rating: D.

FS9-OU

Oh boy! The "Unusual Environments" U generally either means a uselessly-niche underwater variant or a very funny space boarding mech, and we landed on "very funny space boarding mech" this time! Five MPLs. Sword. Liquid Storage Tank for fluff reasons (reaction mass for the jump jets in space). 1,120 BV.

MPL-spamming isn't quite as effective on Inner Sphere mechs as it is on Clan mechs, due to range issues, but the heat here is manageable, and while the close-up damage isn't Locust IIC tier for this BV range, it's spitting out of a much tougher body. My only real complaint is that you can only get two of the MPLs behind you, but back-scratching isn't generally a Firestarter's biggest worry.

Lynn's Rating: B.

FS9-OX

Wait, what's the introduction date on this thing? 3059?!? I genuinely didn't know any of the experimental tech packed into this configuration was being experimented-upon that early. A Streak SRM 2 with one ton of ammo is the only "mundane" equipment in its loadout, paired with a testing loadout of a Large X-Pulse Laser, an Angel ECM Suite, and a Bloodhound Active Probe. 1,190 BV.

I feel like I'm on the cusp of hyperbole here, but this might be one of the biggest beneficiaries of the "Experimental" rules level being retired. (Yes, Battle Cobra X, you're still the greatest, but we're not talking about you right now.) Its damage potential is poor for the BV, but there are only 15 mechs which combine both Angel and Bloodhound, this one has the absolute earliest availability date, it's the fifth-cheapest option out of the list, and it brings the usual Omnistarter mix of decent mobility and decent durability.

The Black Hawk-KU OG is a better option if you can afford it and it exists in your time-frame, since it can actually throw out significant damage and it has thicker armor, but the FS9-OX is literally a game-changer in terms of opening up EWAR tech availability.

Lynn's Rating: B-.

Final Thoughts

There's a reason every single Firestarter I have seen on the table has been playing the role of an Omni Firestarter. This is a significantly better mech than its predecessor in every way other than actually setting things on fire. Technically its art doesn't resemble the BattleMech all that closely, and, as mentioned, it's ten tons heavier, but I promise you that no one will care if you use the regular Firestarter mini. If you absolutely have to differentiate, the Gothic Firestarter sculpt is larger! (The metal Omnistarter sculpt also doesn't look terrible, but it's not their best work, either, and IWM prices recently went up.)

Anyway, it turns out that things like "having armor" and "mounting weapons that can reach further than three hexes" are actually helpful for Firestarters, go figure! Kinda wish more of the 35-ton model's variants had figured that out. (Not like you, Mirage II!)

Until next time, MechWarriors, try to lay off on those self-inflicted mind detonators, eh?

title: Gundam Slingers: Building a Better Clan Deck
content:
Last week, we took a moment to talk about how the meta in the Gundam Card Game had been shaping up with the recent release of Freedom Ascension, and more importantly, a wave of bans and restrictions on various cards and deck building strategies. The Gundam Card Game is still barely a year old, and so meta changes and swings are going to happen more often than not; still, there are a few cases in which things that seemed strong or perhaps never got a great chance to shine can always make a comeback as things swap around. One of those possibilities is the Clan archetype, which primarily focuses around Gundam GQuuuuuuX units and pilots; Clan was one of the second waves of deck types released with the starter decks, and although it had some momentum, the archetype never really dominated like other aggro builds did. With some changes and shake-ups to the types of Units that can be built, though, let’s take a look this week at how to build up from the Clan Unity Starter, and consider how the upcoming September releases might help Clan really take off in the game.

Clan Unity

Clan is best described as a mid-range aggro deck that focuses on card unity and cohesion, and very much wants your deck to be built with the Keyword in mind. Clan is a Red-Green deck, but more importantly, it is a GQuuuuuuX deck; there are quite literally no other Gundam series used in Clan decks, which makes it one of the more flavorful styles of play (assuming you like GQX, which tends to have a mixed opinion). The reasoning for this is primarily due to how most Clan cards call for, dig up, or otherwise interact with other Clan cards; if you’re familiar with Tribal style decks in Magic the Gathering, Clan is very similar to that in how it wants your deck to be almost entirely filled with the Keyword. There is one exception, but we’ll get to her in a bit; this also makes this deck a pretty easy one to start construction on, and overall one of the cheaper decks to build in the Gundam Card Game because of that.

The recent ban/restricted wave also totally misses Clan; the archetype is basically unaffected by any of the changes to deckbuilding that other decks faced, as it doesn’t run the LVL 2 1 Cost Units that many other decks flooded the board with, nor did it use Amuro or Mikazuchi; this is another fun way to consider building into a meta as the deck can take advantage of other players scrambling to rebuild their decks, but it also leads to some weaknesses in the sense that Clan has not had any new cards since the Clan Unity deck and sets released, although that does seem to be changing with some of the upcoming teasers Bandai has released. If anything, building a Clan deck now might also help make your gameplan ready to expand once the newer cards are available, and very likely swap in the needed new cards to replace older ones.

Building Your Clan

Right now, the best overall Clan Deck is the one run by Treminho in May, taking 1st Place at a regional tournament by going 9-0 in the competition. That may seem like bad news in that there haven’t been many Clan placements since then, but frankly the deck didn’t dominate the meta and was mostly an outsider contender, and the recent meta shift has seen people looking to establish what is “the meta” versus experimentation with outsider decks, so I don’t expect to see a lot of Clan decks for a little while longer. That said, I have seen quite a few Red-Green decks splash GQuuuuuuX Omega Psychommu and Nyaan, so the cards are certainly seeing play, just not in their specific “deck” type.

Let’s start with the Units first:

2x Ortega’s Rick Dom (LVL 3 Cost 2)

4x Sugai’s Gelgoog (LVL 3 Cost 2)

3x GQuuuuuu Omega Psychommu (LVL 4 Cost 3)

2x Red Gundam (LVL 4 Cost 3)

4x Red Gundam (Green LVL 4 Cost 2)

4x Red Gundam (Red LVL 4 Cost 2)

3x GQuuuuuu Omega Psycommu (LVL 5 Cost 3) 

4x GFreD (LVL 6 Cost 4)

2x GQuuuuuuX Omega Psycommu (LVL 7 Cost 5) 

4x GQuuuuuuX Omega Psycommu (LVL 8 cost 7)

As you can see, this deck runs a LOT of the same Units, specifically the main bulk of your deck is consisting of Red Gundam, GQuuuuuuX, and GFreD, which primarily nails down the point that this is quite literally the GQX deck more than almost any other deck currently played hews to a specific entity in the Gundam universe.

Ortega’s Rick Dom is a great example of what we’re looking to do with Clan, though, as the card reads: “Deploy: Choose 1 of your other Clan Units. During this turn, it may choose an active enemy Unit with 3 or less AP as its attack target”. The effect itself isn’t amazing or world altering, but it shows that the majority of cards in this deck are going to call for or look for the Clan tag in order to operate. The LVL 4 GQuuuuuuX deals 1 damage to an enemy unit on Deply if you have other Clan units in play, while LVL 4 Red Gundam allows you to deal 2. The synergies in this deck are one of the reasons I enjoy playing it so much (aside from that I like GQX), and I think it makes the game easy to understand and has a very flavorful but fulfilling curve to the deck. If you’ve managed to keep your pressure on and get to the point where LVL 8 GQX hits the field, it can do a massive amount of damage to your enemy’s shields, as well as their units, and will often help swing the game very likely in your favor.

A unit you may have noticed from this list does, however, lack the Clan keyword: GFreD. GFreD and Nyaan both have “Zeon” instead of “Clan”, but there’s very good utility reasons to that. GFreD allows you to deal damage by thinning your trash, and since this deck lacks any way to get cards back from there, it makes for a great way to take advantage of an otherwise unused resource. GFreD is also just a pretty solid beater, and can bully other units fairly effectively in combat to help maintain a clear board.

For Pilots, your deck is going to want to include the 3 main characters from GQX:

4x Amate Yuzuriha (Machu) (LVL 4 Cost 1)

4x Shuji Ito (LVL 4 Cost 1)

4x Nyaan (LVL 4 Cost 1)

All three of these pilots have the Newytype keyword, although at the moment Clan really doesn’t interact with that; and as mentioned above, Nyaan is the one who lacks Clan in her own keyword, but her card does interact with Clan itself by allowing you to remove cards from your Deck to deal 1 damage to an enemy unit. Since your deck is literally nothing but Clan and Zeon, this effect will always activate when you Link Nyaan, making her one of the best cards in your deck despite the fact that she doesn’t inherently use the deck keyword.

Machu allows you to deck fix when linked, letting you see the top card of your deck and either reveal it and place it in your hand, or put it on the bottom of your deck. Since this deck lacks any real draw engine, Machu’s ability is a great way to start fishing for what you want to draw next in your upcoming turns. Shuji has a similar ability, although his activates both when you link AND when you attack, making his ability slightly more valuable than Machu’s, but both will help you cycle your deck try and make getting what you need easier. Gundam really tends to lack heavy draw effects, and almost never anything that shuffles, so having the ability to thin your deck with your pilots is very effective at digging for the thing you really need mid-game.

The final cards in this deck are your Bases, running no Command cards:

2x Clan Battle (LVL 3 Cost 1)

4x Shuji’s Hideout (LVL 3 Cost 1)

Your bases are pretty standard, and perhaps the weakest part of the current deck. Where some of the more meta decks have far more impactful bases, Clan has either Clan Battle, which can give AP+2, or Shuji’s Hideout, which does damage when destroyed (on the caveat that the enemy has to be LVL 4 or lower).

Planning Ahead

Following the release of Freedom Ascension, Bandai already began teasing new upcoming Starter Decks that would come with the next set, specifically Raging Onslaught and Silent Barrage, both of which seem to hint at some new color cards for Red and Green. We’ll have to wait and see if we actually get new Clan cards in these, but some new Red/Green toys for this deck to tinker with would be greatly appreciated, and perhaps the next set will also dangle some newer cards for us.

In the event that Clan is more or less left adrift, that’s not exactly terrible either; if the deck itself won’t work in the meta, there are a lot of other decks that can potentially be built into out of our deck; as mentioned, both of the new coming Starter Decks use either one or both of the colors in this deck, and there’s already quite a few decks that are trying to use Nyaan and Omega Psycommu in various decks, meaning that these cards do absolutely have some life in the current state of the game. Perhaps as we inch closer to September, we’ll start getting more decklists and ideas from these new starter decks, but until then, I urge you to consider giving Clan a try! If you want a solid mid-range color combo or just want to try a new deck, I think Clan is a fun and competitive build that doesn’t require quite as much investment as some of the stronger decks in the meta.
