title: 30th Celebration has a fantastic Base set Charizard figurine, but it's only coming out in one country
content:
I'm starting to get seriously jealous of all the cool, exclusive Pokémon TCG stuff that only comes out in China. It's one thing when it's a sweet SAR card, but now the lucky country is getting a special Charizard box, with a darling figurine that's cleverly modelled on the original Base set card.

The 'commemorative figure gift box' is part of China's product slate for 30th Celebration, and it comes with a jumbo sized version of base set Charizard, marked with the 30th anniversary Pikachu stamp. It also comes with 15 of the anniversary booster packs, which means - as with any Pokémon TCG product that contains cards - good luck to fans trying to get hold of one.

The box comes out September 16, with the rest of this Pokémon TCG set. It costs 780 yuan (about $115) which means that on a price per pack basis, it's not a great deal unless you want the figurine.

Honestly though, who wouldn't? It's a great rendition of an illustration burned into the mind of every 90s-early 2000s kid. I really like how the dark black lines are drawn to make the 3D model match the 2D drawing - it almost looks cell-shaded.

The jumbo card makes it hard to ascertain the model's size from the image. The website states it's 13.3 cm long and 18.7 cm wide, but gives no height measurements. Modern jumbo cards are typically 13.65 × 18.73 cm, so it looks like it's maybe 12-13 cm tall. Base set Charizard is a compact, hunched type of beastie.

These aren't the only 30th Celebration figurines coming out in China. There are also 13 Pikachu figures, each one matching the art of one of the Pikachus from this set. These are far more affordable, selling for about $13.

title: This adorable Warhammer 40k cosplay family will melt your heart like a thermal cannon
content:
One of the challenges of Warhammer 40k cosplay is getting the scale right. If you want to make something massive like a Primarch or Ork Deff Dredd, how do you bulk out your humble mortal frame to look convincingly massive? Most people use plasterers stilts for the extra height, but Scottish cosplay creator Niall Taylor has another solution - suiting up his children Riley and Mya as a diminutive Space Marine Terminator and Sister of Battle puts his own costume nicely in scale.

"My first cosplay with my son was actually a 'Little and Large' Buzz Lightyear set", Taylor says. "I had originally planned to make one just for myself, but once Riley saw it all coming together, he asked if he could have one too", he recalls, "that's really where it all started". From one armored space man to another, the pair moved on to make Little and Large Space Marines. "There was a lot of trial and error involved, but eventually we got there", Taylor says, "it was the beginning of something we could work on together".

Taylor didn't have any similar plans when he started work on his Warhammer 40k Ork Deff Dredd. "This was a much larger undertaking, but it was something I was 100% committed to", he explains. "Halfway through the build, both of the kids started asking if they could have their own Warhammer cosplays."

"I gave them both a couple of ideas, and they chose the characters they wanted", Taylor says, "Riley picked a Deathwing Terminator, while Mya chose an Adepta Sororitas Battle Sister".

"I had to think about how to scale everything so that the costumes would look right while also making sure they were comfortable and practical for the kids to wear", Taylor explains, "there was a lot of trial fitting, reshaping and redesigning involved, but they were always excited to try the different parts on as the builds progressed." The kids got stuck into painting some of the larger pieces.

Though commitments mean it's been a while since the Taylors made it to a con, the family loves them. "There is always a great turnout of children at the conventions, and I'd love to see even more of them getting involved in cosplay", Taylor says. There are reasons why child cosplayers aren't as common as adults. "I think one of the biggest challenges with making costumes for children is the amount of time and effort that goes into them, especially when kids grow so quickly", he explains, "sometimes they might only get the chance to fully wear a costume once before they've grown out of it".

Despite the short shelf life on the costumes, Taylor says "I put a huge amount of time and effort into making sure the costumes are solid, durable and able to stand up to plenty of punishment". All of the family's cosplays are made from EVA foam and hand-painted: "even though they're for kids, I wanted them to be properly made and not feel like they were getting a lesser version".

And that hard work isn't wasted: "after a convention, I normally give the kids' cosplays away", he adds. "I've always liked the idea that someone else might get to enjoy them, and hopefully they might inspire another child - or even another parent - to get involved in cosplay and start making something of their own".

If you want to show off your creative hobby projects, why not hop into the Wargamer Discord community?

title: Competitive Innovations in 11th: Warpmasters pt.1
content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

It's our biggest week of 11th Edition yet, featuring both the Warmasters GT and a GW Open in the UK, plus plenty more besides. It was also the World Team Championships at the weekend, and we're going to have a bonus part covering that next monday (24th August) because there's too much other stuff going on to slot it in during the week.

In terms of the churning metagame, Orks are still on top, but Dark Angels are even closer behind them (really only a hair separates them), and the WTC has unleashed a powerful new force onto the tabletops in the form of Daemons, with Legion of Excess proving to be a serious sleeper that's been fully unleashed as of Warmasters. Archetype

Actual Honest to God Brood Brothers as I Live and Breathe

Thoughts

Brood Brothers. Brood Brothers actually made a top four. I'm not even mad about having to look up what it does for the first time in nearly three years.

Honestly? The synergy here is genuinely kind of sweet. Xenocult has been seeing plenty of play alongside Broodsurge because it gives you the tools you need to set up a few really nasty Neophyte units to cover off shooting support, but there's actually very good support for them from Brood Brothers as well. Hellhounds let them set up Ignores Cover, +1 to hit is (obviously) good for really making the Neophyte swings properly land. You also get solid protection from enemy reserves plans via A Dark Network (and there's lots of +charge Terminators in the metagame right now). Extra punch-up capability from Kasrkin certainly doesn't go amiss either, and what brings the plan together is that the cheap Militarum transports you want for them combine with general Genestealer shenanigans to really lock in Recon scoring. If there's a better example of how much the 2DP+1DP options have opened up list design, I can't think of it, huge props to John.

Both lists are well equipped for that - Sisters have their revivable Characters, while the Aeldari can tearfully feed Warlocks out as required, and benefit from them being OC2, thus trumping solo Sisters pieces till murdered.

Both armies also have some assets that are especially helpful. On these maps, Psychic Shield on a big Dark Reaper unit is especially strong, providing a way of projecting force with minimal response, and being very hard to dodge with teleporting as an option. Being able to teleport the Fire Dragons is also very helpful, as it forces the Sisters to be cautious with Vahl or get her unit instantly blown up, and also makes a tank rush a risky move from the Sisters. They can't be everywhere though, and the crunchier setup from the Sisters side could provide an angle to just bully the table, especially as if the Eldar can only kill Vahl once in a turn, she'll get to go on a prolonged rampage.

What helps the Eldar on that front is that this is one of the missions with the most skewable scoring out there, and even if they get pressured for a few turns, methodically eliminating the foe will allow them to score big later on. That's especially true as either Lhykhis or a teleport can put them straight into position to take big 15VP turns as soon as it's safe. The final thing that tips me in their favour is how good Isha's Fury is in this game - it means that the solo Sisters Characters can lose their first life just as a cost of pushing up to take a point from a Warlock that's about to get shot. That throws off their resource planning, and further helps the Aeldari plan for a big late game swing. My guess with the scoreline here is that both armies skewed their scoring - I'd assume Sisters took early points, and then the Aeldari scored explosively from turn three onwards to close out the game.

title: D&D Arcana Unleashed review - The best 5.5e book so far
content:
Our Verdict

Arcana Unleashed excites me in ways D&D books rarely do. It backs excellent writing up with tried-and-tested rules for subclasses, feats, spells, and factions. While there are many returning subclasses, the book occasionally dares to try something new, and it's better for it. Wizards' campaign frames and design advice are still a weak point, but this only slightly clouds the orb we ponder.

Pros
  • Strong, consistent subclasses
  • Excellent feats and spells
  • Exciting original factions
Cons
  • Dull adventure design
  • Limited design advice

Arcana Unleashed has done something a Dungeons and Dragons book hasn't done for a while. It's made me excited to play D&D. It turns out I do want to play the world's biggest tabletop RPG when the design is consistent, the ideas are original, and the writing is impeccable. Arcana Unleashed has all that in spades.

This might sound like a backhanded compliment, and I guess it is. I have a history of giving Wizards of the Coast 'good but not brilliant' reviews (see Ravenloft: The Horrors Within, Forge of the Artificer, Dragon Delves, etc. etc. etc…). And that's because D&D is the biggest RPG on the planet.

When you lead an industry, my standards are sky-high. I expect you to set an example. Impress. Innovate. Share the most exciting ideas on the market. In recent years, Wizards of the Coast hasn't always met this mark. But I'll give credit where it's due, and Arcana Unleashed is a wonderful little sourcebook.

Most potential buyers will be interested in hearing about the new subclasses. I already gave a full rundown of the winners and losers, but in general, they're quality. Most of the returning options come with a face-lift, though none veer into overpowered territory. One thing D&D has nailed with its 5.5e updates is consistency - imbalance has been addressed from both ends.

We have two new faces in the pack, too: the Warrior of Mystic Arts and the Vestige Warlock. Both have clear strengths and weaknesses. The first, which is basically an Eldritch Knight in Monk form, is powerful but lacks creativity. The second, a Warlock that gains powers from a god trying to regain popularity, is a fantastic character concept, but the delivery is disappointing in places.

The remaining character options are similarly sound. Arcana Unleashed has Origin and Epic Boon feats that could rival those in the Player's Handbook - a first in 5.5e history, in my opinion. D&D has struggled to top these concepts since they were first introduced, but the well of optimal options has expanded.

General feats are eating well, too. Most exciting of all are the new Adept feats, which grant spellcasters a roster of extra spells from a specific school of magic. There's also plenty of feats that modify your Find Familiar spell, making companions a much more exciting part of your party.

There are one or two duds, as always - the lone Fighting Style feat isn't much to write home about. But, on the whole, I'm a big fan. You can see my full list of favorite feats here.

Spells are slightly less explosive. I doubt many of these will break the D&D builds meta (if such a thing exists), but plenty are worthy of your time.

Again, we see some excellent modifications to the party pet through spells like Battle Familiar. I also appreciate that Wizards has tried to improve the laughably bland lineup of Necromancy spells, though I don't think it's enough to save the Necromancer subclass. You can see more of the best new spells here.

From spells, the book moves onto some new ways of framing play. D&D has followed a trend set by some of the best tabletop RPGs and introduced a Patron system. Well, 'system' might be a generous term. There's no unique mechanics to shape the relationship an adventuring party has with their benefactor.

Rules-wise, Patrons manifest as a series of random tables defining their personality and method of contacting your characters. Each 'type' presented (Archmage, Esoteric Institution, Magical Entity, Political Faction, Trickster, and Wizard Circle) also has suggested motivations and perks to offer. Lastly, D&D offers one of its characteristically un-fleshed-out campaign frames - a list of bullet points suggesting what might happen at different tiers of play.

It's not enthralling from a rules design perspective, but excellent writing saves the Patron section. It's in-depth enough to spark plenty of ideas in a budding DM.

We see the same in the next section, detailing brand-new factions. Brand-new! So much of Wizards of the Coast's product strategy in recent years has involved recycling ancient settings and characters - so when I saw something that looked original, I nearly jumped out of my seat.

And the factions are really cool. There's magical whisper networks, eldritch transmuters, morally upstanding necromancers, planar globetrotters, and an Indiana-Jones-like spy network that steals and protects magical artifacts. There's even a band of evocation casters who hang out to perform sick stunts and make things explode (and sometimes help out at sites of natural disaster).

Each faction has different goals and rewards they'll offer you for allying with them. Here, Arcana Unleashed expands some of its optional rules from the Dungeon Master's Guide. Each faction has a Renown meter that offers increasingly useful benefits. Plus, members of a faction unlock access to a unique Bastion facility.

The factions have it all - strong ideas, written well, that are backed up by tangible mechanics. They have me genuinely excited to dream up some new D&D adventures.

The next chapter on magic items is more of a mixed bag. There are some decent new options at all rarity levels (see my full rundown for more detail). Nothing feels like it's going to revolutionize D&D, and maybe that's a good thing, but this section rarely sparks joy for that reason.

Plus, I have a bigger gripe, and it's with the new evolving magic items. The idea of magic items that grow as their owners level up is a fantastic one. Arcana Unleashed provides a few useful examples, too.

What it doesn't provide is practical advice on creating your own well-balanced options. The design advice begins and ends at 'roll on our small randomized table'. In a world where fans have written entire books on playing and designing D&D well, Wizards can do better than gatekeeping how the sausage gets made.

Last of all, we have new monsters. Most of the page count is made up with Archmage variants for each school of magic. These are structurally almost identical, albeit with different spell lists (and, for some reason, the Abjurer gets fewer attacks, and is the only one that can't cast Shield as a reaction). This is handy stuff for anyone who wants a ready-made Archmage Patron, but it feels a little bland outside that context.

We also have Groundlings, a new subset of minions for your big bad, Darkenbeasts mutated by magic, and Living Spells, which have developed a will of their own. On the higher end of CR comes good-aligned steward liches, magically ascended mages, and literal Venger himself. These are solid and well-designed (though I still long for the days when bosses could cast spells properly), but they're not standout enough to be the book's main attraction.

That's all on Arcana Unleashed for now? Though, if you want to chat more about D&D, you can often find me lurking in the Wargamer Discord.

A review copy was provided by Wizards of the Coast for this article.

title: MTG fan menaces local game night with 6-foot-tall deck of 2000+ cards
content:
A basic rule of Commander is that your deck must have 100 cards (99 and one commander). But one of MTG Mystery Booster's rulebreaker cards, Whtz, The Bibliophile says screw that, and lets you go wild, building a deck just as large as you like.

While most players would choose to craft a 240-300 card deck and then try and find a way to win with Battle of Wits or Triskaidekaphile, one loose cannon has decided to push things to the extreme, bringing a legal EDH deck of over 2,345 cards to their LGS's Commander night. Look, it even has its own custom-built deck box, and it's six feet tall!

According to the deck's creator, they were inspired by the infamous 2007 German Nationals Yugioh deck, Mission Impossible - a 2,222 card deck which a player brought to a tournament to demonstrate why a max deck size was required. "Being able to bring that to MTG seemed like a fun project," they say.

When this story was posted online at the beginning of the week, the reaction was varied, with a lot of disagreements about whether a deck of this size violates rules related to slow-play or shuffling (and what those rules actually are, if they exist) but the player claims they can actually shuffle it in reasonable time.

It "does not take 45 minutes, which feels like a good bar", they say, adding that there were even times where they'd be done shuffling before the next player had finished their turn. They also argue it didn't hinder the game - only themself.

Rather than being stuffed with duplicate cards like Templar Knights, the 2,345 deck is "just fun Azorius cards".

"The deck allows you to run so many more cards than you normally would, so you get to see more than just the same ol' 500 EDH staples," says its maker.

Many would assume (or at least hope) this was a one-and-done sort of situation - the person who shared the pic even stated that the LGS regulars enjoyed the experience, but would probably only do so once. However, the deck's creator describes it as "an ongoing project" and plans to bring the beast to more game nights in the future.

They say, "Worst case, it's a big ol' box that you can see from across the room, so pretty easy to avoid."

What's the strangest deck you've encountered at an LGS - and does this sound like your idea of a fun time, or a nightmare? Share your thoughts over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: The rarest and most expensive Lorcana cards of 2026
content:
What are the rarest, most expensive Lorcana cards? When the characters and films are so beloved by so many, it only makes sense mega-fans are prepared to shell out for a rare Disney card with unique art of their favorite character. This guide covers all the most expensive Disney Lorcana card sales from the most recent sets.

Disney Lorcana may be the newest of the big trading card games, but it has a dedicated fanbase of collectors who will pay a princess' ransom to get their hands on the most coveted cards. Older TCGs may have higher price ceilings - nothing on this list can match the most expensive rare Pokémon cards or expensive Yugioh Cards - but there are some very valuable cards nonetheless! The most expensive Lorcana cards are:

Elsa, Spirit of Winter (Enchanted) - $935

The original Elsa from 2023's The First Chapter set is already a collectible card, but this full art Enchanted variant is in another league. She's a double threat - not just one of the most popular Disney characters of all time, but the first card printed of that character when the game launched. If you've got one, don't let it go…

Hades, Looking for a Deal (Iconic) - $967

This is currently the rarest Disney villain card around! Though released alongside the next character, Pocahontas in winterwear, and just as rare, this card has had a slower rise to the heights. Maybe it's because Hades isn't a princess? Still, this sneaky backstabber has been closing the distance all August, and now he's breathing down her neck.

Pocahontas - Peacekeeper (Iconic) - $969

The incredible multi-colored foiling on this card really does paint with all the colors of the wind. Pocahontas has never looked so noble - or so snug in that gorgeous coat!

Moana, Curious Explorer (Iconic) - $1,143

Moana was a surprise appearance in Winterspell, a set with a Winter theme, and it seems this explorer's curiosity is so great she didn't have time to dress for the colder weather. Nevertheless, this paper-cut inspired artwork is absolutely adorable, and helps to make this Iconic card so legendary.

Winnie the Pooh, Hunny Wizard (Enchanted) - $1,289

The colors here are making us so hungry. Pooh Bear doesn't have any fancy abilities to show off, but he does have a soothing smile, a fancy cloak, and golden, sugary goodness surrounding him. Those base stats aren't too shabby, either. Pooh bear and Moana keep jockeying for position with very similar price points.

Ariel, Ethereal Voice (Iconic) - $1,344

This ghostly 'Whisper' of Ariel from the Whispers in the Well set not only has a commanding performance, she also commands a high price on the secondary market, which has only crept up since she released.

Lilo and Stitch, Fun-Loving Friends (Iconic) - $1,682

There's so much energy and mischief in this Lilo and Stitch card. It looks like the box art for a straight-to-DVD sequel to the classic movie, and we mean that with love: there's no way any actual animation could live up to the sheer action this promises!

Merida - Formidable Archer (Iconic) - $1,844

We all know that Lorcana is a pacifist game, and nobody involved in a challenge is ever hurt - but we have to wonder what Merida does with her arrows to keep her opponents from getting hurt! This is one of the most dynamic princes poses in all of Lorcana - and one of the few princesses to ever cost more than Minnie Mouse (though the royal rodent has since regained her throne).

Belle and Beast, Certain as the Sun (Iconic) - $2,189

A card as romantic as this was destined to be sought after - Belle and Beast waltzing is a timeless scene from the film that kicked off the Disney Renaissance.  They're also remarkably faithful to their original on-screen appearance as well.

Minnie Mouse, Sweetheart Princess (Iconic) - $2,244

When the first Iconic cards were created for Lorcana they were immediately way pricier than anything else on the market, and nearly made it into the all-time top 10, up against extremely rare early promos. Minnie, blowing a kiss in her medieval princess garb, was beginning to slip from her initial high position on the list - but made a recovery in late August as a sheer lack of supply drove up the market price.

Mickey Mouse, Brave Little Prince (Iconic) - $2,658

But, of course, Mickey was always going to do better than Minnie. So far, this card bucks the Lorcana card trend, with its price and hype only rising over time - and as there are fewer copies in the wild and sales have slowed down, by the end of July it had crept over $2,500.

Buzz Lightyear, Jungle Ranger (Iconic) - $3,593

The price for Buzz Lightyear has practically gone to Infinity and Beyond! When Wilds Unknown released it quickly became the second most valuable card you can open in a booster pack - and now it's surged ahead of the iconic Mickey Mouse. This run might be about to end, however, as at the time of this update the market price has ticked down ever so slightly - perhaps because the best quality copies of the card have found their forever homes, leaving only cheaper versions on the market.

If you're a Lorcana collector but not yet a player, you should fix that immediately! It's easy to learn, and we can talk you through which Lorcana starter decks are worth playing.

title: Games Industry News Roundup- August 18th, 2026
content:
Here at Tabletop Battles, we know that it’s hard to keep track of all the news happening all the time in the games industry. So much is always going on, all over the place, all the time. With games of all sorts, and their related media, being an informed gamer can feel impossible some days. 

That's why every week, we help you stay in the know by rounding up five of the biggest recent stories in the gaming and gaming-related pop culture sphere in the Games Industry News Roundup. Our trusty news boy, Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson, is right here at the very real, and cool TTB newsdesk with the scoop.

Credit: Games Workshop

Games Workshop Quietly Raises Prices for Warhammer Products

Bad news for Warhammer fans this week, as a hobby known for being expensive is getting even more expensive. Games Workshop announced in a trade update that they would be increasing the prices of many of the paints and models across all their systems this September.

According to the document found on the Warhammer Retailer’s Network website, this price change is set to take place on September 26th, and the changes are between 3 and 5 percent on average. 

In the past, Games Workshop has released articles on the Warhammer Community website or on their social media platforms announcing the price change, but at time of writing the company hasn’t put out any official word regarding the change. It should be noted however that this information comes directly from the Retailer Network, and it's common for retail outlets to get news of pricing changes before the general public.

While some serious external factors that would necessitate a price increase do exist, such as the ongoing conflict in Iran, Games Workshop has been increasing the prices of Warhammer products for multiple years in a row now. While these changes are individually very small year to year, they’ve substantially added up. With this upcoming price increase, kits will cost around 25% more than they did in 2022, when the pattern of these annual increases first began.

Image credit: Games Workshop

Dawn of War 4 Delayed Into December

Even more bad news for Warhammer fans this week! You hate to see it.

With just a little over a month before its wide release to the public, the team behind the highly anticipated Warhammer RTS Dawn of War 4 announced that the game would be delayed from its original September 17th release to a new December 3rd release.

In a video released by the studio behind the game, King Art Games, Creative Director Jan Theysen addressed the decision to push the game back so significantly.

"As we approached the final stages of development, we saw an opportunity to further enhance Dawn of War 4 and deliver the quality of experience we’ve always envisioned," said Theysen. "The additional time will allow us to continue optimising performance, resolving bugs, and applying further polish to ensure players have the best possible experience from day one."

The updated release window does also skirt an extremely packed September release window, as many triple-A titles like Marvel’s Wolverine, The Blood of the Dawnwalker, and Control Resonant have crammed into the month to avoid the titanic release of GTA VI in November. 

In addition to the new release date, King Art Games released the updated roadmap taking the delay into account. With the new roadmap, DLC rollout for Dawn of War IV will start in 2027, with the Blood Ravens prequel expansion dropping in the spring followed by a full expansion pack with a new faction later in the winter. Fans who’ve preordered Dawn of War IV will also have early access to the title starting on November 30th.

Credit: Gen Con

Gen Con Brings in New Head of Events as Convention Attendance Grows

Gen Con, like many other tabletop related conventions, is in the middle of an attendance boom, and the team behind the biggest weekend in tabletop gaming is hiring a new Head of Events, Camilla Cleghorn, to assist in wrangling the rapid growth of the show. 

Cleghorn is already a notable figure in the tabletop world even prior to her joining the Gen Con team as one of the main presenters for The Dice Tower, a media company focused on reviewing board games and creating video, article, and podcast content about tabletop gaming. Cleghorn is also responsible for organizing Dice Tower East, a gaming convention hosted by The Dice Tower in Florida, as well as managing various crowdfunding campaigns for the company. 

“From the publisher and exhibitor side, I’m fortunate to come in with experience working closely with many of those partners, but I don’t want to arrive with a list of things I think need to change before I’ve had the opportunity to listen and learn,” Cleghorn told Boardgamewire in an interview. “Gen Con has an experienced team and a tremendous community of partners. My priority will be understanding what’s working well, where opportunities exist, and how we can continue to build on that together.”

Cleghorn will work closely with former Director of Events Derek Guder, who will be transitioning into a different role at Gen Con, and leaving her position at The Dice Tower to work for Gen Con full time.

This year’s Gen-Con attendance was an all time high of 74,000, beating the convention's previous record of 72,000 last year and continuing the upward trend in the convention's popularity, with seemingly no sign of stopping.

Credit: Saber Interactive

Head of Saber Interactive Apologizes for Remarks Made about Former Writer

Saber CEO Mark Karch bravely removed his head from his ass last week after firmly jamming his head up his ass earlier in the same week. 

Early last week, Karch snapped on social media regarding the claim by former Saber writer Stella Sacco that she was fired from one of Saber’s projects and replaced with an AI writer. 

“Stella who? I had to ask Claude because I have never spoken to her or seen her. We have already said we are using AI for certain parts of the game and will update the Steam page once we have finalized the feature set.” Karch wrote in a statement. “As far as Stella is concerned, she was replaced by someone more talented and terminated for a variety of reasons a few months later. From what I can gather she enjoys controversy even more than I do. I would frankly in retrospect have been happy to replace her with AI. At least we would be dealing with someone programmed to be honest.”

Understandably, this response drew widespread criticism, including from Sacco herself. “I've seen the statement by Matt Karch, the CEO of Saber Entertainment, and all of the truly horrendous things he said about me,” she wrote on social media. “I think it should be obvious to anyone who reads that statement that he's lashing out because he did not want people to know there was AI use in the game.”

Following the backlash to Karch’s statement, Saber Interactive added an AI tag for the upcoming release of their game, Rideshare “Simulator” on Steam, which the company had previously refused to publicly acknowledge. Karch addressed his improper behavior on his LinkedIn and apologized to Sacco privately, with Sacco acknowledging that she had received an email from Karch where he regretted his words and for escalating the situation. 

Sacco says that while her position against AI in games writing is unchanged, she does accept Karch’s apology in good faith. 

Credit: Smilegate/Amazon Games

Amazon Passes Ongoing Operation of Lost Ark to a New Dev Studio

Struggles continue in the world of gaming over at Amazon, as Amazon Game Studios-run MMO Lost Ark announced that the game’s ongoing maintenance and new content will be handed off to the games primary development team Smilegate.

“Starting in early 2027 Amazon Game Studios will end its live service operations of Lost Ark, with Smilegate taking over going forward.” the Lost Ark team writes in a blog update. “We are excited about the future of Lost Ark and feel this is a positive outcome for the game's players, as we are handing the game back to the developers. This way, their passion for Lost Ark will live on and players can continue their adventures in the world of Arkesia.”

Smilegate, the South Korean development team behind Lost Ark, released the game locally in 2018 before partnering with Amazon for a wider North American and European release in 2022. With the transition of Lost Ark’s live service content in the west to Smilegate in early 2027, Smilegate will control all aspects of operations for the popular MMO in both the Korean and Western markets.

Amazon notes that the team is working diligently to make the transition to Smilegate as smooth as possible for western fans of the game, saying that all previous game and character data will transfer to Smilegates servers without any issues. While most things will transfer, some others will be lost in the transition, such as chat logs and player blacklist memos, and Amazon Games encourages payers to back these up while they have the chance.

This is just the latest in a long trend of Amazon Games axing its live service ambitions, with the company cancelling a Lord of the Rings MMO last year and announcing that it would be shutting down the servers for its breakout game, New World, in January 2027.

title: Kings of War Fracture Focus: Basileans - For the Glory of the Hegemon!
content:
G’day Tabletop Battles readers! After a few weeks marinating with the new Kings of War Fracture book, we are excited to share our opinions regarding the most fanatical human faction in the Kings of War world - the Basileans. As we shared in our Fracture book preview, the Basilean army list received a lot of exciting updates, from expansions to their lore to a whole swathe of new Command Orders and many interesting developments to the army list. Let’s dive in and see why the Hegemon of Basilea is worth fighting for!

Basileans armies are made up of a core of human soldiers. Credit: Mantic.

The Lore

The Basileans are the fantasy Eastern Roman Empire (aka the Byzantine Empire) that continued on after Primovantor (the fantasy Roman Empire) literally drowned due to magic-induced climate change. Like the Roman Empire, Primovantor was a vast grand empire of humans, famed for its well-equipped and well-trained legions and ruled over by the Hegemon (the Emperor).

The comparisons to the Romans fall apart, however, once we get to the true formation of Basilea as it is in current Kings of War. Unlike the Romans, when the Basileans were facing annihilation at the hands of ravening hordes and they prayed to the gods, the gods (the Shining Ones) listened and intervened. Warrior angels known as Elohi swept down from the heavens, and celestial powers were bestowed upon the heroes of Basilea. Where in our history Constantinople fell, the City of the Golden Horn of Basilea grew and prospered.

The dedication of the Basileans to the Shining Ones changed the culture of the empire forever. Orders of paladin knights and sisterhoods began forming to defend the faith, which were quickly brought into the military machine of the Basileans to supplement the legions. War priests wielded the celestial power of the gods, healing and purging in equal measure. To the dismay of all the enemies of Basilea, even the Elohi and Phoenixes regularly support the Basilean armies.

The Phoenix is considered one of the great Mantic models in the Basilean range. Photo credit Mantic Games

Despite the prosperity of Basilea, it has a constant need to maintain its fighting forces thanks to its proximity to the hellish Abyss. It does not help that within Basilea there is a schism of religious doctrine, and it threatens to destabilize the region. The whole problem is based on what to do about the Wicked Ones of the Abyss, the evil counterparts to the Shining Ones.

Traditionally, the Basileans were all for the detainment or even destruction of the Wicked Ones; however, recently there has been a growing movement to see the Shining Ones and Wicked Ones reunite and reform as the Celestians they once were. No one is certain this is possible, but some of the Shining Ones think they are strong enough to overcome their Wicked halves, and that’s enough for their supporters.

This is all covered in the Fracture book; however, to really get an insight into the Basileans, you can read the Sacred Ark series of books by Mark Barber which bring the world to life, starting with Steps to Deliverance. The books cover all manner of viewpoints throughout the empire, from common foot soldiers, to paladins (Orion), and even a half-human half-elohi known as Aestelle (both of which feature in the new army list). These books show just how good and bad the Basileans are.

Steps to Deliverance is the first novel in a series about the Basileans, featuring Orion and Aestelle. Credit: Mantic

Command Orders

For the Glory of the Hegemon

For the Glory of the Hegemon is a simple enough order; charging unit gains Elite (Combat). It’s good enough by itself but where it really shines is when combined with a Bane Chant from the War Priest. Giving some Paladin Foot Knights Elite AND Crushing Strength (+1) will turn them from mild threat to vengeance of the Shinings Ones made manifest. Will you get this combination off every time you need it? Unlikely, but when it does happen, the Abyss will cower (and your opponent will shudder). The name is also very flavourful, and one should definitely bellow it (politely) in a Hollywood Roman accent (see Gladiator [2000]).

Cleanse

Cleanse gives a unit Iron Resolve (+1), which is not shabby by itself but is not exactly as good as a Heal. This reflects a general reduction in Command Orders that directly heal units; instead the healing is conditional on it actually surviving a Nerve Test.

The real boon of Cleanse is that it removes any ongoing effects of spells, such as Weakness, Frozen, Scorched Earth or Hex. Many armies' entire strategy relies on reducing the effectiveness of enemy units, and Cleanse is one of the only means to overturn it. Paladin Knights are being Hindered by Scorched Earth, not anymore! This won’t always be a useful Command Order, but it is invaluable in the right situation.

Aegis of Kolosu

Now first off, everyone is wondering who or what is a Kolosu. Answer: It's the mountain upon which the Shining Ones reside in Basilea; essentially Mount Olympus. Hopefully that helps.

Regarding the command order itself, it bestows Faithful units with +1 Defence against ranged attacks in the front facing. This is almost identical to the old Forces of the Abyss Command Order but differs in one key way - the units it can affect.

The Forces of the Abyss order was limited to Upper Circle units, of which there were not many to choose from and none of them were the ones you wanted to protect from shooting. In contrast, the Aegis of Kolosu can affect Faithful units which are almost all the units in the army list; Men-at-arms, Paladins, Sisterhood. The fact that it is also issued on a roll of 4+ rather than the Abyssal’s 5+ makes it much more reliable. Prime targets are Paladin Foot Knights and Paladin Knights, getting their Defence to a mighty 6+ against shooting.

Borne by Angels

If the sole purpose of Command Orders was to bring out the uniqueness of each army, then Borne by Angels is perfect. A Infantry or Large Infantry unit gets Fly when moving (not charging). Angels sweeping down in a blaze of bright light and whole units of Paladins fly across the battlefield.

Blocking terrain in the way? No problem! Need to fix up some bad deployment? Just fly everything around until it fits! Enemy in the way? Not anymore! This will be the Command Order that will surprise opponents the most, as units move into places they weren’t supposed to get to.

Ogre Palace Guard can be potentially flown across the battlefield by angels... which would look quite funny considering an Elohi is slightly smaller in stature. Photo credit Mantic Games

Fell the Beast

For the simple minded (such as yours truly), Fell the Beast is the most satisfying of the new Basilean Command Orders; an Infantry or Cavalry unit gets Slayer (+nD3 - Combat), ‘n’ being the number of successful dice rolled in the issuing. The fact that this is PLUS Slayer is what makes it nice and spicy, because there are a few powerful units in the Basilean army list that have Slayer (D6) already, and adding another 1-3 D3 on top of that can turn that unit into a real can-opener! We cannot wait to have that one battle (it will likely only happen once) where our Paladin Monster Slayers have Slayer 12.

Spells

Holy Lance

The new spell exclusively available to the Basileans in Fracture is Holy Lance, a literal laser beam of holy radiant damage that starts off strong and tapers with distance. It has Piercing (1) and Shattering (1), and at 12” and below gets to roll 9 dice to hit. If going for 24” you get 7 dice and up to 36” you get 5 dice.

At this point in 4th edition, all offensive damage spells must be compared to Blizzard (3), and the Holy Lance compares favourably depending on the situation simply because it is not classed as a Magic Missile. It hits on 4+ no matter what (with the exception of Spellward), and means that your War Priest need not sit still to get that bonus to shooting. It can keep up with the army and issue the great Basilean Command Orders. Obviously the range from target will determine if it is better or worse than Blizzard (3) in terms of damage output, but overall Holy Lance works better with the army. If you really want to shoot the enemy off, then just take another War Priest with Blizzard (3) and have the best of both worlds.

Core and Auxiliary

Paladin Monster Slayers

The Paladin Foot Knights of the Basileans are already pretty tasty, but running the Defense 4+ variant in order to get Crushing Strength (2) is a bit precarious for a regiment of Nerve 17+. Paladin Monster Slayers fix this problem by giving you the horde of infantry, pushing their nerve to a very respectable 24+ and giving them Slayer (D6) to boot. This is the unit that will terrify your opponent, and this is the unit you should do everything in your power to keep healthy, with all the Heal, Iron Resolve, Cleanse, and Celestial Restoration you can muster. Then when it gets into combat hit it with the one-two combo that is Bane Chant and For the Glory of the Hegemon (or Fell the Beast, depending on the enemy) and watch the enemy break like a fart in the wind.

Of course, there remains the difficulties inherent in most hordes of infantry. It can be unwieldy. It’s a major target for ranged attacks. It’s a lot of points. But Orcs players happily invest in hordes of Greatax, and they are on massive Heavy Infantry bases, so if anything this is easy mode, especially with the awesome Command Orders. And unlike Orcs, in Basileans, Infantry can fly…

Specialists

Order of the Abyssal Hunt

That’s not it for massive hordes in the Basileans, because they get something even bigger: The cavalry horde, in the form of the Order of the Abyssal Hunt. This unit has been taken from the former Order of the Brothermark, which in the lore were steadily being absorbed by the Basilean armies. Now they are represented as a giant cavalry horde (which is the same size as an Orc horde) with a very decent profile. Where regular Paladin Knights have Thunderous Charge (3), the Order has Crushing Strength (1) and Thunderous Charge (2). Like the Monster Slayers they come with Slayer (D6), which makes them situationally devastating (sorry Ogres). The real downside to this unit versus the regular knights is that by being a Unique unit, they are unable to take magic items, the key one being Sir Jesse’s Boots of Striding, to ensure at least one charge they make is not Hindered. That is unfortunately the fate of most cavalry hordes, charging while Hindered, so at least they have Crushing Strength (1) to help with that. This is definitely a unit to take because you love the idea of massive cavalry charges, but not if you want the most efficient use of points (360 of them!) or an easy to use unit.

Champions

Aestelle

Coming straight from the Sacred Ark series of books, Aestelle is one of the main characters, an ex-Sisterhood initiate with Elohi blood in her veins. She’s a decent close-combat hero with 5 Melee 3+ attacks with Crushing Strength (1), Elite, and Vicious. She even has a bow attack, but alas no Elite and Vicious for that. The main downside is she lacks Inspiring, which would make including her a difficult choice were it not for the Aura (Iron Resolve (+1)). Everything in the army has Iron Resolve, and bumping that up to a baseline of (2) is nothing to sneeze at. Combined with the Cleanse Command Order and suddenly units are healing 3 damage every time they pass a Nerve Test. This doesn’t make her auto-include, but it at least means she has a use despite the lack of Inspiring.

Aestelle is available as an STL from the Mantic Vault and myminifactory. Credit: Mantic Games

Orion

Orion is a character followed throughout the Sacred Ark books, from his tragic beginnings as a hopeless squire, to the battles as the implacable paladin he became. This is represented in Kings of War as one heck of a combat character. His basic stats are pretty standard among combat characters - Speed 8, Melee 3+, Defense 5+, 5 attacks with Elite and Crushing Strength (2). There’s no doubt Orion can do some damage, but he excels in a manner few other heroes truly excel - fighting other heroes.

It’s no secret that Duellist in fourth edition is a rather lackluster rule. It grants a bonus number of attacks when attacking a hero unit, typically just D3. Getting 1 to 3 extra attacks is hardly enough to take down most enemy heroes, and most often the kinds of units that have Duellist lack Inspiring, making them even less desirable a choice. Orion not only has Duellist (D3+2), giving him the potential of hitting with 10 attacks, but he also has the unique special rule Disarm. If he hits an enemy hero, they suffer from the effect of Weakness. Couple this with the fact Orion has Inspiring and we have a unit worth having!

Orion is available as an STL from Mantic Vault and myminifactory. Credit: Mantic Games

Warlords

Abbess

The first of the Warlords of the Basileans to be tweaked slightly, the Abbess’s stats haven’t changed, but the way she affects the overall army has. Now she touts an Aura (Brutal (+1 Sisterhood only)) as well as making Sisterhood Panther Lancers into Core choices. In short, if you want an army full of Sisterhood units, then this is the Warlord for you. Unfortunately, it means that outside of that niche, she has not much applicability compared to the other Warlords. She might be the cheapest Warlord, but certainly not the most useful.

High Paladin

Like the Abbess, the High Paladin hasn’t changed much, but crucially has gained a unique ability called Holy Edict: The ability to issue Command Orders up to 15”. Considering how good, but in some cases situational, the Basilean Command Orders are, having a Warlord capable of covering a 30” bubble of the army is incredibly useful. On top of that, the High Paladin makes regiments of Paladin Knights Core choices, freeing up those Specialist slots for units like the Ogre Palace Guard. Almost any Basilean army can benefit from having the High Paladin as a Warlord. Strangely, when the High Paladin mounts a dragon, they lose the Holy Edict ability. Maybe it’s hard to hear the commands with all that wing flapping and roaring.

Samacris Mother of Phoenixes

Samacris, the spellcaster Elohi hero, has also changed subtly. She no longer interacts with the Elohi, but rather the Phoenix, granting them the ability to take the spell Martyr’s Prayer (5). This spell enables the transfer of damage from a friendly unit to the caster for each success rolled, essentially the Phoenix can soak up damage. This spell was previously available only to the War Priest, who has a pretty low ability to soak up damage before expiring. The Phoenix on the other hand not only has much higher Nerve, but also boasts Regeneration (4+), making it capable of taking advantage of this spell in a way no other unit could.

Samacris might cost a lot of points, but her utility cannot be denied. Credit: Mantic Games

Gnaeus Sallustis

Gnaeus disappeared at the advent of fourth edition, but now he’s back with a very happy new model. He’s an exceptional combat hero with 7 attacks with Crushing Strength (2), a hefty Nerve 17+ with Iron Resolve (1) and Fearless, and Speed 9. He cannot be ignored but he is also quite hard to remove. This would already be a nice package for the 240 points he costs, but he also has Master of the Field, the ability to issue two Command Orders a turn. One Warlord, two Command Orders, incredible value.

Gnaeus is a very good warlord for any Basilean army. Credit: Mantic Games

My Army List: The Silversaints of San Michon

Over the course of writing this article, I quickly found a lot to like about the Basilean army list. It’s got a lot of simple humans just trying to fight the evil of the world, but enhanced with holy magic that can really make them all superhuman.

This got me inspired to start a Basilean army with the idea of recreating the forces that feature in the book series Empire of the Vampire by Jay Kristoff. If you haven’t read Empire of the Vampire, I heartily recommend it for all that appreciate an epic set in a post-apocalyptic medieval vampire world. In fact, I want to thank the hosts of Unplugged Radio (a Kings of War podcast) for mentioning it.

Empire of the Vampire, an excellent book series for any lover of dark fantasy. Can also recommend the audiobook. Credit: Jay Kristoff

The whole reason for mentioning the Empire of the Vampire is the holy order of half-vampire vampire slayers called Silversaints that feature in the book. Their vampire fathers have imbued them with unholy strength, and the Order of San Michon collects these half-vampires and trains them to be vampire slayers, lest they instead give in to the sanguine hunger. When I saw the new unit of Paladin Monster Slayers, I knew these to be my Silversaints.

The rest of the army simply came together to reinforce the theme. Paladin Knights, Men-at-arms, Sisterhood, all of these are found in the world of Empire of the Vampire. The only unit that isn’t present in that world are Elohi, so my army is notably lacking the more angelic units on offer in the Basilean army list. I will likely introduce them with time (mayhaps if Mantic remakes them?), but for now they are out.

The central power of this army are the two hordes - the horde of Paladin Monster Slayers and the Order of the Abyssal Hunt. The army needs to act as a delivery mechanism for these hordes to ensure I get value on investment.

For Monster Slayers there are the Men-at-arms regiments (both the spear and crossbow wielding variants), which will precede the Monster Slayers in a manner similar to the Roman quincunx formation. This formation enables the independent units to support each other when engaged, the only tricky part is that this takes a lot of space to work optimally and not every table’s terrain will be so facilitating.

On that note of space, the cavalry horde that is the Order of the Abyssal Hunt will be the hardest to use well. Units like Orion and the Gur Panthers will be escorting them, tying up enemy units, but it might not be enough. Of course, it will be difficult to avoid terrain on the charge, but thankfully the Abyssal Hunt has that critical Crushing Strength to help them. Watch this space, as this is the part of the list that will change the most.

Finally there’s the ranged pressure to force engagements. Most of the army is not fast, but the two cannons, crossbowmen, Sisterhood Scouts and the Holy Lance of the War Priest should be enough to get the enemy moving.

It’s not a typical Basilean army, but it is one I am very excited to make. All the units will be Mantic with the exception of the Paladin Monster Slayers, which I have taken to Titancraft to make some Silversaint models. Silversaints are so called because of the silver tattoos that adorn their body, so I am in for a ridiculous level of free hand (which is not something I typically do).

What armies do you, dear readers, have in mind? One festooned with Elohi and Phoenixes? Or perhaps it’s all about getting as many Ogre Palace Guard? Let me know on the socials, I am keen to read them!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Magic: The Gathering's treasure-making talent card sees 300% price rise
content:
The Magic: The Gathering card Alchemist's Talent has shot up in price over the past week. It's risen from about $5 on the secondary market to $19, a pretty speedy increase of 280%.

There's an obvious reason why Alchemist's Talent - and other strong treasure cards like Rain of Riches and Bottle-Cap Blast - are moving up in price. The Hobbit set just came out, and it has three very popular versions of Smaug that all care about treasure.

Alchemist's Talent is strong in all three of the Smaug decks, and all three have contributed to the spike. But its seeing particular consistent play in Smaug, the Magnificent - where it's logged in 70% of the decks on EDHREC.

There are a couple of likely reasons why this Smaug wants to utilize the talent of alchemists more than most. For starters, it's mono-red instead of black-red, so it has a far smaller card pool in general.

But secondly, Alchemist's Talent's best effect is to make your treasures twice as effective - they all generate two mana once you hit this class card's second level. That's very solid on a commander that is constantly generating treasures, one at a time.

Smaug, the Magnificent wants you to build up a critical mass of treasures as fast as possible, so it's probably the most treasure-focused version of this set's commanders. This mana ramp card will therefore help you cast more treasure-making spells more quickly. It also means you won't need to burn quite so many treasures to cast your spells, helping you maintain a healthier horde with which to hurt your opponents.

This isn't the first time Alchemist's Talent has spiked, but the third. It became one of the most expensive cards in Bloomburrow shortly after its release, simply by being one of the better cards you can run in a very popular archetype.

The reason it rose after that - at the very, very end of 2024, is mysterious to me. At first I thought it might have something to do with the Sonic Secret Lair cards, each of which works pretty well with treasures. But, no, in fact these weren't revealed until halfway through 2025, so it must be Foundations that set the card spiking. Rev, Tithe Extractor is mono-black, so it wasn't her…. Nope, I'm afraid I'm stumped.

At least this particular spike is less mysterious! Keep an eye on other red or black treasure cards you might happen to own. Odds are, all the best ones are seeing some movement.

title: 5 old board games I'm still playing, because overconsumption is uncool
content:
I review board games as a full-time job. I'm very lucky to do so, but the need to constantly stay on top of 'what's hot' can take its toll. Sometimes, I glance at my review copy pile of very new, very exciting games, and I start asking questions. Questions like 'how many of these will I still want to play in 10 years' time?'

Much of the tabletop industry is propped up by overconsumption. Kickstarters live and die on their capacity to sell you not just a shiny game, but FOMO. Hell, sites like this one survive because consumers want to know what the best board game or Warhammer army or Magic: The Gathering card is RIGHT NOW.

There is always something new and exciting to buy, and personal collections can quickly bloat. I own so many board games that playing them all regularly is simply unfeasible. I may review them for a living, but I have several friends who've bought their way into the exact same situation.

I'm not here to decree that we all stop buying board games. There's lots of new ones that deserve your attention. I do, however, want to take pause. Put the breaks on your relentless desire for The Future of Gaming, and take stock of what you have now.

What games have you held passionate love affairs with for many years? Which will never leave your life? Which are you still playing after all this time? Here's mine:

Azul

First published: 2017
Years in collection: 4 years

I play Azul several times a week, either at the tabletop or in my browser. It comes out every Christmas. Despite the simplicity of its drafting and tile-placing, I never seem to run out of brain-teasing turns. There's a richness to its decision-making. Combined with the approachable playtime, and you've got an instant classic.

Azul will turn 10 next year, which makes it basically ancient for many modern gamers (don't @ me if you're older than 10 and offended). My personal copy is still in good nick, however, as I picked it up not long after Covid. A Christmas gift I received not long after getting my job at Wargamer, it represents a moment where board games became a bigger part of my life than ever before.

Mysterium

First published: 2015
Years in collection: 9 years

Mysterium released right before I went to university, and I discovered it while studying my Bachelor's. The spooky concept - mediums trying to discover how a ghost was murdered through cryptic visions - instantly clicked with this card-carrying goth. Even better, the gameplay is as smooth as it is silly.

I still whip this one out for my family, but when I first found it, I was a fresh-faced young adult in an unfamiliar city. The uni board game society became my main source of friends. I met one of my dearest friends there, and as a huge fan of image-association games like Dixit, she introduced me to Mysterium. Recently, I was a bridesmaid in her wedding. Thanks, Mysterium!

Dead of Winter

First published: 2014
Years in collection: 10 years

Dead of Winter hit the scene back when we were still using words like 'Ameritrash' to describe thematic board games. It's a full-on beer and pretzels game where you work together to gather resources, murder zombies, and try to survive a harsh winter. There's narrative elements, as well as a hidden traitor mechanic.

Sure, it's not remembered as fondly as games like Eldritch Horror, Nemesis, or the more recent Unfathomable. But I'm a die-hard defender of it, and I still play it regularly. I remember Dead of Winter as one of the first 'hobby' board games I ever bought - and the first my zombie-loving parents would actually play with me.

One Night Ultimate Werewolf

First published: 2014
Years in collection: 12 years

Another of my first purchases as a hobby gamer was One Night Ultimate Werewolf. The breezy, five-minute game of secret murder and pointing fingers was my first introduction to social deduction, now my favorite board game genre. It might be the game that got me hooked on board games, as well as Carcassonne (a classic that's still in my collection, too, but more for sentimental reasons).

12 years later, One Night Ultimate Werewolf is just as accessible and addictive as it ever was. I use it as an icebreaker game, a drinking nights game, or a gateway to get people to play my new all-time favorite game, Blood on the Clocktower.

Yahtzee

First published: 1956
Years in collection: 25+ years

Forgive the odd orientation of this one photo - it was taken by my mom. The Russell family have been playing Yahtzee for literally as long as I can remember. That's almost 30 years! The box disintegrated long ago, but we still have the sheets and the dice cup.

For me, no roll-and-write has ever surpassed Yahtzee's satisfying simplicity. Maybe my judgement is clouded by emotions.  I certainly look back on family Yahtzee nights with warm, fuzzy feelings. It was the board game I played when I was still learning my numbers. It might be the first tabletop game I ever touched. And, yes, I still play it today.

Want to share your own lifetime board game list? I'm all ears in the Wargamer Discord.

title: Best tabletop RPGs 2026
content:
The Wargamer team has spent years learning, testing, and breaking TTRPG systems, and we've played everything from old school D20 fantasy systems to indie journaling games. These are our recommendations for the best TTRPGs that you should know about, no matter what you're on the lookout for.

Read on for our list of the all-time great tabletop RPGs. And, yes, before we begin, Dungeons and Dragons is on the list. However you feel about its massive monopoly on the hobby, the influence of DnD classes and DnD races simply can't be ignored.

The best tabletop RPGs are: 

  • Dungeons and Dragons
  • Blades in the Dark
  • Mörk Borg
  • Call of Cthulhu
  • Pathfinder
  • Warhammer 40k: Imperium Maledictum
  • Star Wars Roleplaying Game
  • 13th Age
  • Night Witches
  • Ten Candles
  • Daggerheart

1. Dungeons and Dragons

Dungeons and Dragons is the original tabletop RPG, with 50 years of experience under its belt. Combining strategy with some flashy magic and charismatic heroes, it remains the bread and butter game for sword-and-sorcery fans searching for a fantasy-based RPG. While it started out with strategic wargaming roots, the latest edition is as much about storytelling as it is power-building.

Its rules are of middling complexity, as far as RPG systems go. You build a character using classes, races, feats, and spells, and you use their skills (and a trusty d20) to navigate combat and exploration scenarios. It's complex enough that you can dive very deep into its mechanics, but the core gameplay is simple enough that new players can get by without having read the Player's Handbook cover to cover.

D&D clearly has some staying power, but what I'm about to say next is quite controversial: this is my go-to TTRPG for beginners to the hobby.

Yes, the RPG has its rough edges, with rules that aren't always as clear or easy to find as they could be. Learning how to play can be pretty intimidating without a guide to point out the essentials.

But the sheer size of the community around the game means it's still the best point of entry. No other RPG has so many community-made resources and helpful explainer videos. Not to mention the sheer number of players out there - if you want to find a group to join, D&D is absolutely your best shot.

2. Blades in The Dark

Blades in The Dark is a heist game where players form a crew of scoundrels embarking on ever more daring scores in a world without sunlight. Set in the fictional gothic, industrial city of Doskvol, the RPG launches you into an exciting crime-caper gameplay style, facing off against rival crews while avoiding the law.

At the same time, you must try to survive volatile Victorian back alleys where ghosts roam and lowlife citizens are ready to stab you in the back, and your own decisions inevitably come back to bite you. All that is delivered with fast, easy-to-pick-up game mechanics and unique character choices.

From the 'flashback' system - which lets you decide how to prepare for a heist after you've gotten there - to the option to play as a ghost after a character's death, Blades in The Dark constantly rewards you for inventive roleplay and imaginative thinking, while requiring little setup or preparation. It works for both one-shots and lengthy campaigns, and will suit those who want to get stuck into a detailed story with minimal prep time.

3. Mörk Borg

Let's make one thing clear: you're going to die. A self-described doom metal album of a game, Mörk Borg ain't for the faint of heart - in its apocalyptic world, the rules are light and the consequences for simply existing are heavy.

Created by a couple of ingenious, deeply disturbed Swedes named Pelle Nilsson and Johan Nohr, Mörk Borg is filled with serpent-worshiping cultists, insidious cannibals and deadly miseries. GMs roll daily to determine if a horrifying prophecy will be fulfilled, and once seven have occurred the universe ends.

If you're thinking this sounds like the bleak, macabre, occult energy of a Scandi horror flick, in RPG form, you aren't far off. With its dark aesthetics, medieval Nordic setting and headbanging character classes like 'heretical priest', if you're a fan of heavy metal music, you're going to love Mörk Borg.

The rules are fat-free, focused on getting you stuck in and giving the players and GM the maximum leeway for experimentation. Combat is fast and lethal, and players only have four stats and maybe a couple of abilities - all the better to roll up a new character when you inevitably die.

4. Call of Cthulhu

A cosmic horror and investigative saga that will almost certainly end in your character going insane, Call of Cthulhu is one of the most well-known and beloved tabletop RPGs on the market. The game takes place in the world of H.P. Lovecraft's endlessly popular cosmic horror novels, and turns players into investigators, traveling through a 1920s setting full of paranormal and mind-bending mysteries.

Playing as a squishy investigator, violence is a last resort, and most encounters with eldritch horrors require rolling desperate, quick-thinking skill checks to escape their clutches. The game is incredibly well supported with well-designed adventures and campaign supplements, riffing on the works of Lovecraft and his contemporaries.

It's also worth noting that even if you don't succumb to Lovecraftian madness, you will probably die nonetheless, making it the perfect game for one-shots, or groups who love getting to grips with an RPG's rules through multiple playthroughs - and don't mind rolling up multiple new eccentric turn-of-the-century weirdos over the course of a campaign, to replace the characters lost to the Great Old Ones' machinations.

5. Pathfinder

When Dungeons and Dragons 4th edition was announced, Paizo - who at the time published the official magazines Dungeon and Dragon - launched Pathfinder as a continuation of the D&D 3.5e rules. In the years since the first edition Pathfinder has evolved into a unique game with its own identity and dedicated fanbase.

Pathfinder is for gamers who love crunch. It's got heaps and heaps of classes, ancestries, spells, and other player options - if you can think of a character concept, you can find a way to stat it.

This can be a little overwhelming at first, but the reams of rulebook actually give you an enormous amount of freedom. The level of detail in every character, magic item, and adventure makes levelling up a unique build really satisfying.

Plus, Paizo regularly releases interesting setting books and adventure paths to help players explore the canon Pathfinder world, Golarion. It's one of the rare RPGs with an advancing metaplot, where major supplement releases can really shake things up for your characters

6. Warhammer 40k: Imperium Maledictum

Warhammer 40k: Imperium Maledictum is a fantastic and fairly recent roleplaying game set in the grimdark Warhammer 40,000 universe. A powerful Patron has gathered the player characters together, pulling them from lives of servitude within one of the Imperium of Man's colossal institutions to direct them to their own ends.

The Patron system is a very versatile roleplaying tool. While the game master can decide on a patron for the group, this can be a collaborative activity, letting the players set the tone for the campaign. A Patron from the Inquisition will see the players delve into heretical cults and forbidden tomes, while a Rogue Trader master might see the party shipping from world to world in pursuit of profit.

You even get to customize your Patron, picking a set of bonuses that you can use in your adventures - perhaps they can lend you a squad of shock troopers as back up in fire fights, or maybe their deep ties with the Adeptus Administratum will allow you to descend on a 'legitimate' business with a team of auditors. But the more benefits you pick, the more secret flaws the game master will give them as well.

The game uses a d100 system and handles investigation, social scenes, and combat remarkably well, and even manages to mesh them together. The more you can uncover about an enemy before you engage them in combat, the more 'superiority' you will accrue, which turns into a flat bonus on every roll once combat starts. This ensures that parties with more bookworms than bruisers aren't disadvantaged when the grox dung hits the fan.

40k lore can be intimidatingly deep, but the core rulebook does an excellent job introducing the setting as a whole - you don't need to have read all the Horus Heresy books to understand the game, as a player or as a GM. The self-contained Macarian sub-sector of the Imperium is vividly described, and full of ready-to-use adventure hooks for GMs.

7. Star Wars Roleplaying Game

The Star Wars Roleplaying Game has you step into a galaxy far far away, joining a crew of heroes traveling the (apparently incurably) war-torn galaxy that once belonged to George Lucas.

The game is broken up into three distinct modules: Age of Rebellion, Edge of the Empire and Force and Destiny. Age of Rebellion sees you taking up the insurrectionist cause, becoming a rebel fighter in their guerrilla war against the Empire. Force and Destiny (if the name didn't clue you in) treads the Jedi path, having your characters learn the way of the force. Finally, in Edge of the Empire, you take your cues from Han Solo or Boba Fett, smuggling, bounty hunting, and essentially swindling your way across the Outer Rim.

No matter which of these games you choose, they're smoothly compatible with one another, as they all share the same core rules and mechanics, meaning you can easily cross over between the modules and engage with the 'full experience' - if your wallet can stretch to all three sourcebooks. The general game mechanics are simple, and perfectly capture the fast-moving, unrestrained gameplay you'd expect from a Star Wars RPG.

8. 13th Age

13th Age is a parallel universe cousin of Dungeons and Dragons. It was created by two former D&D lead designers, Jonathan Tweet (the lead author for D&D 3rd edition) and Rob Heinsoo (a lead designer on D&D 4th edition), to use for their home game. It hits all the same notes as D&D, but the way it plays them is much more interesting.

The core of the game is a recognizable, D20-based fantasy RPG, with a party of heroes from a variety of fantasy races and classes who venture into the unknown in search of adventure. Every character has "one unique thing", something that makes them stand out from everyone else in the world. It doesn't have to be big and powerful - you might just be the winner of the dwarven Adamantine Chef competition - but it is something that the bards will sing about once your character is famous.

Combat is snappy, thanks in part to the 'escalation die', a d6 that ticks up every round of combat and provides all of the players a bonus to hit, and unlocking more potent abilities as the fight goes on. The game comes with a default fantasy world known as the Dragon Empire.

The most notable beings in the world are the Icons, powerful and archetypical entities like the Archdruid, the Liche King, and the Protector. Each character has a narrative connection to one or two Icons, injecting complications and benefits for the party throughout the adventure. Picking which Icons you want to be connected to, and how, is a great way to signal to the GM what kind of game you want to be part of!

9. Night Witches

In Night Witches, you and your friends will play as pilots in the Soviets' famed all-woman air force, bombing Nazis during the night and navigating the politics and relationships of the male-dominated Red Army by day. Creator Jason Morningstar (the designer behind popular card-driven storytelling game Fiasco) has splashed a heavy mix of history and combative tension into this WWII tabletop RPG.

The game has two distinctive modes built into its night-and-day cycle. At night, you engage in deadly aerial combat, making strategic decisions as a team to complete missions in your two-person aircraft. During the day, you are a roleplaying master, avoiding NKVD interrogation and getting ready for the next night's combat sorties.

Night Witches makes it easy to figure out if you prefer combat-heavy or narrative-focused RPGs, since it ably simulates both styles - letting your group discover what kind of roleplayers they truly are, all while enjoying the game's strikingly well-done war story.

10. Ten Candles

Cavalry Games' Ten Candles is, hands-down, one of the most atmospheric games I've ever played. A one-shot-only game, sessions take place in a dark room, with ten candles providing the only source of light.

At least, that's how the game starts. The candles aren't just there to set the mood; they're a core part of the RPG's mechanics. Players have a communal pool of d6s they must roll any time they face a conflict. If the roll fails, a candle goes out. When the party are down to their final candle, the group must narrate how they die. They can choose to burn the paper they've written parts of their character on to improve their chances, but Ten Candles only ever ends one way: darkness and death.

Storytelling comes before everything in Ten Candles. The rules are very light, and the Game Master doesn't have sole control of the narrative. They'll often be rolling against the players, with the winner getting to narrate the outcome of a roll.

If you've only ever played games like D&D, Ten Candles can be a little jarring at first. The social contract between DM and players is totally different, and there's no real way to 'win' a scenario or build a powerful character. However, if you love telling a good (but grim) tale, you can't do better than Ten Candles.

11. Daggerheart

Daggerheart is a heroic fantasy that's all about weaving cinematic, collaborative narratives. Whether you want a whimsical world of sentient frogs and mushrooms frolicking in forests, or elves and dwarves battling through a grimdark dungeon, Daggerheart can help you craft the world and stories of your dreams.

System-wise, Daggerheart is asymmetric. Game Masters roll D20s and spend Fear points accrued in play to influence the world, while players roll dual D12s, aiming to gain the Hope points that fuel the coolest powers on their class cards. That's right, cards - character creation involves shuffling two decks together and hand-picking your favorite upgrades.

Daggerheart's greatest strength is the way it encourages collaboration. GMs can get players involved in the story setup, from drawing up campaign maps together to simply asking how many legs a new monster has. It adopts many great mechanics from other, established RPGs in a way that feels familiar yet fresh - and heaps of fun.

Looking for more game night ideas? Ask us for more recommendations in the Wargamer Discord community - our Tabletop RPGs channel pops off every day with Wargamer readers sharing new games to try, homebrew ideas, and more.

title: Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Brings Slavic & Balkan Folklore to Life in a New Fantasy TTRPG Setting
content:
Eren Chronicles has launched Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch, a new tabletop role-playing game setting inspired by Slavic and Balkan folklore, on Kickstarter. The campaign, which went live on Tuesday, has already surpassed $120,000 in funding within its first day, making it one of the most notable Dungeons & Dragons 5e campaigns of the year.

Zamanora transports players and Dungeon Masters into a world of rural communities, dark forests, and vengeful witches. The setting is designed to support both Wizards of the Coast’s Dungeons & Dragons 5e and 2024 editions, as well as Legend In The Mist, the rustic fantasy RPG from Son of Oak Game Studio that was recently voted the Most Anticipated TTRPG of 2025.

The Zamanora setting draws heavily from Slavic and Balkan folklore, offering players a chance to explore a world where cautionary tales come to life. Players can create characters from fantastical local creatures such as the mischievous Chorts and the spectral Huants. The setting also introduces unique subclasses, including the Bogatyr fighter, Guslar bard, and Hearth-domain cleric, allowing for thematic storytelling deeply tied to the region’s traditions.

Two new magic systems are introduced in Zamanora: Poppet Magic, a manipulative form of spellcasting, and Ceremonial Magic, which enables non-casters to perform magical rituals. These systems provide fresh ways for players to engage with the game world.

The setting features a variety of mythical creatures familiar to fans of Slavic and Balkan folklore, such as the leshy, baba yaga, and kikimora. These beings are joined by a host of other monsters, each accompanied by detailed descriptions and lore.

The Zamanora Kickstarter offers a range of rewards for backers, from digital PDFs to deluxe collector’s editions. Pledge tiers include options for digital content, physical books, and various accessories. The Core, Deluxe, and Collector’s Boxes include items such as dice, a GMless adventure deck, Baba Yaga miniatures, a DM screen, a monster deck, an illustrated slipcase, and a hand-knitted plushie.

A free demo of the Zamanora setting is available for download on the Kickstarter page, allowing potential backers to explore the world before committing to a pledge.

For more information or to support the project, visit the Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Kickstarter page.
